citation: Aleksandr Algasov, Ekaterina Nepovinnykh, Fedor Zolotarev, Tuomas Eerola, Heikki Kälviäinen, Pavel Zemčík, Charles V. Stewart. "Unsupervised Pelage Pattern Unwrapping for Animal Re-identification." arXiv:2506.15369 [cs.CV], announced 19 June 2025.
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CV). NOTE: the input record's claim of 'accepted to AAAI 2026' could NOT be verified and has been REMOVED from the citation.
license: unknown — no public code repository located
representation_3d: 2.5D geometry-aware texture mapping, NOT a fitted 3D template mesh. Per-pixel surface-normal estimation guides an unwarping of the pelage pattern into a canonical UV space, with a stated objective of preserving geometric consistency between the 3D surface and the 2D texture space. There is no shared template mesh and no UV atlas of one — confirming the input record's characterization.
species_domain: Saimaa ringed seal (Pusa hispida saimensis) and leopard (Panthera pardus). Mammals only. No fish, no elasmobranch.
supervision: Self-supervised. Abstract states explicitly: 'Our framework does not require ground truth UV annotations and can be trained in a self-supervised manner.' Requires a surface-normal estimation component; segmentation is implied but not specified in the abstract.
key_numbers: 'Experiments on seal and leopard datasets show up to a 5.4% improvement in re-identification accuracy' — this is the single headline number, and it is an improvement delta over a non-unwrapped baseline, not an absolute accuracy. No absolute top-1 figure was accessible.
data_requirement: Not stated in any source I could reach. Images per individual, number of views, resolution, training set size and GPU-hours are all unavailable — the arXiv abstract page and PDF were unreachable (see correction_note), and only the abstract text was recoverable.
elongate_relevance: medium — seals are the closest published body-plan analogue (fusiform, limb-reduced, laterally deformable) and the method is template-free so it does not inherit a joint-tree assumption; but a hauled-out seal photographed dorsally is near-developable, whereas a free-swimming sevengill in large-amplitude lateral undulation is not, and the paper does not address that regime.
correction_note: TOOLING CONSTRAINT, stated for honesty: arxiv.org, huggingface.co, semanticscholar.org (site and API), dblp.org, ar5iv, alphaxiv, openaccess.thecvf.com and proceedings.neurips.cc are ALL blocked by this session's network egress proxy, and the WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before I issued a single query. I therefore could not fetch the arXiv abstract page directly. CORRECTIONS MADE: (1) The input record's venue claim 'reported accepted to AAAI 2026' is UNSUBSTANTIATED — it was self-flagged in the record as coming from an unverified search snippet, and I found no evidence for it; it must NOT appear in the final report as a venue. Cite this as an arXiv preprint. (2) The input record's date of 'Jun 2025' is confirmed correct. (3) code_url confirmed empty: I searched GitHub repositories for 'pelage pattern unwrapping', 'pelage unwrapping animal reidentification', 'Saimaa ringed seal re-identification', and 'UV unwrapping animal re-identification surface normal canonical', and searched GitHub code globally for the exact strings 'Unsupervised Pelage Pattern Unwrapping' and '2506.15369' — the ONLY hits for either string were arXiv-scraper mirror repos (flyingbitac/daily-arXiv, TipD4/daily-arXiv). citation: Maria Stennett, Daniel Rubenstein, Tilo Burghardt. "Towards Individual Grevy's Zebra Identification via Deep 3D Fitting and Metric Learning." IEEE/IAPR International Conference on Pattern Recognition Workshop on Visual Observation and Analysis of Vertebrate and Insect Behavior (VAIB), August 2022. arXiv:2206.02261.
license: NONE FOUND — no LICENSE file and no license statement in the README. I fetched both the repo landing page and the raw README and confirmed no license is declared. Under default copyright this means all rights reserved: do NOT vendor this code without written permission from the authors. SEPARATELY AND MORE IMPORTANTLY, the pipeline depends on SMALST (github.com/silviazuffi/smalst), whose own code is MIT BUT which ships LICENSE_SMAL_MODEL.txt — a Max Planck 'Software Copyright License for non-commercial scientific research purposes' governing the SMAL model itself. I fetched that file: it states 'Any other use, in particular any use for commercial purposes, is prohibited... This license also prohibits the use of the Data & Software to train methods/algorithms/neural networks/etc for commercial use of any kind', and forbids redistribution ('shall not be copied, shared, distributed, re-sold... except that you may make one copy for archive purposes only'), with commercial licensing via ps-license@tue.mpg.de. Any SMAL-derived template route for sevengills inherits this NON-COMMERCIAL, NON-REDISTRIBUTABLE encumbrance.
representation_3d: Full canonical-surface pipeline, confirmed from the repo README's own four-stage description: MegaDetector v4.1 detection -> species classification -> deep 3D model fitting via SMALST (SMAL + learned texture) -> individual ID by deep metric learning (triplet loss on a ResNet) over the pose-invariant texture extracted onto the template surface.
species_domain: Grevy's zebra (Equus grevyi). Quadruped mammal, rigid-ish torso.
supervision: MegaDetector v4.1 (pretrained) + a species classifier + pretrained SMALST (which itself requires a species-specific 3D template and synthetic training data) + individual identity labels to drive the triplet loss.
key_numbers: 56.8% identification accuracy on the SMALST dataset. CRITICAL ADDITIONAL FINDING from the README, not present in the input record: 'Each animal side requires separate classification due to distinctive pattern differences' — i.e. even after fitting a 3D template and unwrapping to texture space, the left and right flanks are NOT unified into one identity representation. The claimed viewpoint-invariance of the UV route is therefore partial, and this directly weakens the central premise of the sevengill proposal.
data_requirement: CONCRETE, from the repo README: evaluation used 4 unique images of each of 37 individual Grevy's zebras (=148 images), formed by combining the SMALST test and validation sets, photographed at The Great Grevy's Rally 2018. So: ~4 images/individual, 37 individuals, single-camera opportunistic photographs (not multi-view rigs). Image resolution, GPU-hours and SMALST retraining cost are NOT STATED in the README; SMALST's own synthetic-data training requirement is inherited but unquantified here. Note the identity training set is tiny — 148 images is far below what the lab's 4850-file/661GB white-shark corpus could supply, so data volume is not the binding constraint; template quality is.
elongate_relevance: low — a zebra torso is close to rigid and the coat sits on a near-cylindrical barrel, the friendliest possible case for template unwrapping. Its value here is as a CAUTIONARY CALIBRATION, not a body-plan analogue: this is the closest published instantiation of the exact architecture proposed for sevengills, and at 56.8% it materially underperformed contemporaneous 2D pattern matchers on the same species. Since its error budget is dominated by template-fit quality, an anguilliform, laterally undulating hexanchiform with no published template will do worse, not better.
correction_note: MATERIAL CITATION ERROR CORRECTED — the input record's third author was WRONG. The record listed 'Tanya Y. Berger-Wolf' (self-flagged as 'inferred... treat names as probable'). The actual third author is TILO BURGHARDT (University of Bristol). I verified this against the authors' own BibTeX block published in the official repo README (raw.githubusercontent.com/Lm0079/grevys-zebra-individual-identification/main/README.md), which reads author={Stennett, Maria and Rubenstein, Daniel and Burghardt, Tilo}. The middle author is given as 'Daniel Rubenstein' without the 'I.' initial in the authors' own citation. Had this record gone into the final report unchecked it would have been a misattributed citation. Title, venue (IEEE/IAPR ICPR Workshop VAIB), month (August) and year (2022) are all CONFIRMED correct as given. The arXiv ID 2206.02261 is corroborated by the repo README's own reference to it, but note I could not fetch arxiv.org itself (egress-blocked, see the algasov record's correction_note), so the ID rests on the repo's own linkage rather than on the arXiv abs page. Repo owner is GitHub user Lm0079, identified in the README as Maria Stennett — the repo is authoritative for this citation.

citation: Rıza Alp Güler, Natalia Neverova, Iasonas Kokkinos. "DensePose: Dense Human Pose Estimation In The Wild." IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2018. arXiv:1802.00434.
license: CC BY-NC 4.0 — exact string: 'Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International Public License'. VERIFIED by fetching raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/DensePose/main/LICENSE directly. This is NON-COMMERCIAL and is decision-relevant. The successor implementation, detectron2's DensePose project, is under a DIFFERENT and permissive license: I fetched raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/detectron2/main/LICENSE and confirmed 'Apache License, Version 2.0, January 2004'. Practical guidance: use the detectron2 DensePose project (Apache-2.0), not this archived original (CC BY-NC 4.0), for anything that might become commercial. Note also that a permissive CODE license does not license the DensePose-COCO annotations or the SMPL body model, which carry their own terms.
representation_3d: Part-index plus (u,v) 'IUV' regression onto a fixed SMPL body surface partitioned into 24 charts. The canonical archetype of the pixel-to-canonical-surface technique.
species_domain: Humans only.
supervision: Fully supervised on DensePose-COCO: ~50,000 images with MANUALLY annotated image-to-surface correspondences. This annotation burden is the crux of the whole proposal — there is no elasmobranch equivalent and no plausible way to crowdsource surface correspondence on a shark.
key_numbers: DensePose-COCO: ~50K annotated images. 24 surface charts on the SMPL template. Precise AP/GPS benchmark figures were not recoverable — the CVPR open-access page and arXiv were both egress-blocked (see correction_note).
data_requirement: ~50,000 manually surface-annotated images for the supervised route; annotation is per-pixel-to-3D-surface correspondence collected via a purpose-built annotation pipeline. Images per individual is not a meaningful axis here (this is pose estimation, not re-ID). Resolution and GPU-hours: not recoverable from sources I could reach.
elongate_relevance: low — human topology with articulated limbs and a 24-chart layout built around them. Nothing in the chart decomposition transfers to an anguilliform trunk. Its relevance to the sevengill question is as the cost benchmark that the proposal must answer: who annotates the (u,v) correspondences, on what template, and at what scale.
correction_note: The input record was CORRECT on authors, title, venue, year and arXiv ID — all confirmed (the repo landing page independently attributes the work to Güler, Neverova and Kokkinos, CVPR 2018). The record's stated GAP has now been CLOSED and its speculation corrected: it said the license 'type is not stated on the landing page', guessed 'a custom FAIR non-commercial research license', and explicitly asked that the LICENSE file be verified because raw.githubusercontent had not been fetched. I fetched it. The actual license is a STANDARD Creative Commons BY-NC 4.0, not a custom FAIR license — the record's non-commercial instinct was right but its guess at the license family was wrong, and a report claiming a 'custom FAIR license' would have been inaccurate. Additional verified fact not in the record: this repository was ARCHIVED on 31 October 2023 and is read-only; the maintained successor is the DensePose project inside detectron2 (Apache-2.0). Confidence downgrade to note: I verified license and archival status from the repo, but could NOT fetch the arXiv abs page or the CVPR open-access page for this paper, so the reported benchmark metrics remain unverified.

citation: Natalia Neverova, David Novotny, Vasil Khalidov, Marc Szafraniec, Patrick Labatut, Andrea Vedaldi. "Continuous Surface Embeddings." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2020.
license: Apache-2.0 — VERIFIED by fetching raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/detectron2/main/LICENSE, which reads 'Apache License, Version 2.0, January 2004'. This is the PERMISSIVE option in this record set and is the one to prefer over the original DensePose repo (CC BY-NC 4.0) and over anything SMAL-derived (Max Planck non-commercial). Caveat: Apache-2.0 covers the CODE; pretrained model-zoo weights and any template meshes or correspondence annotations may carry separate terms not stated in that file.
representation_3d: A learned per-vertex embedding on a 3D template mesh plus a per-pixel embedding predicted from the image; matching the two yields dense pixel-to-template-vertex correspondence. Crucially, pose-invariance is LEARNED in embedding space rather than solved via an explicit articulation model.
species_domain: Humans, chimpanzees, and a general 'animals' category. Confirmed from the official model zoo entries in DENSEPOSE_CSE.md: R_50_FPN_soft_chimps_finetune_4k, plus R_50_FPN_soft_animals_finetune_4k and variants trained on ds1_train / ds2_train. No fish or elasmobranch models exist in the zoo.
supervision: Sparse 2D-to-3D keypoint/vertex correspondences. The official documentation confirms a class-agnostic training mode 'where all annotated instances are mapped into a single category', and points to cycle-loss bootstrapping via the companion CVPR 2021 paper. Far cheaper than DensePose-COCO's dense manual annotation.
key_numbers: No benchmark numbers verified — the NeurIPS proceedings page and arXiv were egress-blocked. What IS verified from the official repo documentation is the model zoo composition (chimp and general-animal CSE models at R_50_FPN, 4k finetune schedules) and the class-agnostic training option.
data_requirement: Not stated in the sources I could reach. What is structurally required, and is the load-bearing point for the sevengill question: a TEMPLATE MESH for the target species, plus some sparse vertex-correspondence supervision. The lab already has a shark template asset (DigitalLife3D great white, 3912 verts) but it is the WRONG SPECIES — a lamniform, with five gill slits, two dorsals and a lunate caudal. A sevengill needs its own mesh: seven gill slits, a single posterior dorsal near the pelvics, an elongate strongly heterocercal caudal with a long upper lobe, a broad blunt head, and a longer more flexible trunk. Sourcing or sculpting that mesh is the unbudgeted prerequisite for this entire route.
elongate_relevance: high — this is the strategically most important record in the chunk. Because CSE learns correspondence rather than modelling articulation, it needs NO joint tree, which means the lab's 16-keypoint white-shark schema failing to transfer to a hexanchiform (no second dorsal, dorsal set far posterior, seven gill slits rather than five) is NOT fatal to this route the way it is fatal to a SharkSMPL/LBS-style route. The bending-parameterization problem is sidestepped entirely. The real costs are elsewhere and should be stated plainly: a sevengill template mesh must be obtained, correspondence supervision must be created, and CSE guarantees only correspondence — it gives no area-preserving or isometric atlas, so the UV space it produces is not metrically faithful and identity patterns will be locally distorted by an unknown amount.
correction_note: CONFIRMED with no changes required — the strongest record in this chunk. I fetched the official primary source, raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/detectron2/main/projects/DensePose/doc/DENSEPOSE_CSE.md, and the BibTeX there matches the input record's author list, order, title and year EXACTLY: @InProceedings{Neverova2020ContinuousSurfaceEmbeddings, author = {Neverova, Natalia and Novotny, David and Khalidov, Vasil and Szafraniec, Marc and Labatut, Patrick and Vedaldi, Andrea}, journal = {Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems}, year = {2020}. The Apache-2.0 license claim is also now verified from the LICENSE file rather than assumed. NEW LEAD SURFACED, worth adding to the scan as a separate record: the same official doc cites the cycle-loss companion paper — Natalia Neverova, Artsiom Sanakoyeu, David Novotny, Patrick Labatut, Andrea Vedaldi, 'Discovering Relationships between Object Categories via Universal Canonical Maps', CVPR 2021 — which is the mechanism for transferring canonical maps ACROSS species without per-species dense annotation. That is directly on-point for bootstrapping a sevengill canonical map, and the input record set does not contain it. I verified its existence only via this official BibTeX block, not via its own arXiv or CVPR page, so it should be re-verified before citing. One honesty caveat on this record: the record's 'url' field points at the code repo rather than at a paper page; I left it as given because the NeurIPS proceedings page and arXiv were both unreachable from this session, so I could not supply a verified paper URL.

citation: Artsiom Sanakoyeu, Vasil Khalidov, Maureen S. McCarthy, Andrea Vedaldi, Natalia Neverova. "Transferring Dense Pose to Proximal Animal Classes." CVPR 2020, pp. 5233-5242. arXiv:2003.00080.
code_url: https://github.com/asanakoy/densepose-evolution (docs/README stub only — NO code, NO LICENSE); actual implementation shipped in https://github.com/facebookresearch/detectron2/tree/main/projects/DensePose
license: asanakoy/densepose-evolution: none found — repo root contains only docs/ and README.md, and /blob/master/LICENSE returns HTTP 404. The usable implementation lives in facebookresearch/detectron2, whose LICENSE I fetched and read: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0), commercial use permitted. CAVEAT: the chimp CSE assets (chimp_5029.pkl mesh, geodists, symmetry, phi_chimp_5029_256.pkl LBO basis) and the pretrained weights are downloaded at runtime from dl.fbaipublicfiles.com and carry no separately stated license in the repo — verify before any commercial use.
representation_3d: Two variants, both verified in the detectron2 DensePose docs. (1) Chart-based: transfers the human SMPL 24-chart IUV atlas onto chimpanzee instances, which are annotated under the `person` category — i.e. it literally reuses the human chart atlas. (2) CSE (Continuous Surface Embeddings): a species mesh `chimp_5029` (5029 vertices) with a 256-dimensional Laplace-Beltrami-operator (LBO) eigenfunction embedding (phi_chimp_5029_256.pkl), predicted per-pixel and matched to mesh vertices. The CSE route is the pose-free canonical-surface mapping the sevengill proposal actually needs; the chart route is not reusable off-human.
species_domain: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), plus the broader DensePose-LVIS animal set used for the `soft_animals` initialization (bear, cow, cat, dog, elephant, giraffe, horse, sheep, zebra — all mammals, all quadruped/biped limbed topology).
supervision: Weak/near-zero target-class supervision: a self-/pseudo-labelled bootstrapping pipeline from human DensePose plus off-the-shelf detectors and segmenters, with a small sparse human-annotated set (~3 point correspondences per instance) for finetuning and evaluation. No 3D ground truth, no multi-view, single monocular images only.
data_requirement: VERIFIED from projects/DensePose/doc/DENSEPOSE_DATASETS.md and the released config. DensePose-Chimps chart-based: 930 instances / 654 images, 6 MB json, VALIDATION ONLY. CSE splits: densepose_chimps_cse_train = 500 instances / 350 images; densepose_chimps_cse_val = 430 instances / 304 images. Annotation density: ~3 annotated points per instance (dp_x, dp_y, dp_vertex) plus an RLE foreground mask — i.e. roughly 1,500 point correspondences total to train a whole new-species CSE head. Finetune recipe densepose_rcnn_R_50_FPN_soft_chimps_finetune_4k.yaml: ResNet-50 FPN, MAX_ITER 4000, LR steps (3000, 3500), embedder NUM_VERTICES 5029 / FEATURE_DIM 256, initialized from the soft_animals CSE checkpoint. Reported cost: 0.569 s/iter train, 4.7 GB train memory, 0.051 s/im inference — 4000 x 0.569 s is about 38 minutes wall clock, though DENSEPOSE_CSE.md does NOT state the hardware, so call it roughly 0.5-5 GPU-hours. Accuracy: GPS 32.2, GPSm 39.6. Views per individual: single-view monocular, not applicable (this is not identity work). Image resolution: not stated in the chimps config; inherited from Base-DensePose-RCNN-FPN.yaml.
elongate_relevance: low — the finetune cost is trivially affordable (~350 images, ~3 points each, under an hour of GPU) but the mechanism that makes it cheap is topological proximity to the source class, and a hexanchiform has none: no limbs, no chart atlas correspondence, and no pretrained aquatic CSE to initialize from. Every existing CSE reference mesh is a limbed mammal.
key_numbers: DensePose-Chimps 930 inst / 654 img (chart, val-only); CSE 500 inst / 350 img train, 430 inst / 304 img val; ~3 points/instance; chimp_5029 mesh, 256-d LBO embedding; 4k finetune iters, 0.569 s/iter, 4.7 GB, 0.051 s/im; GPS 32.2 / GPSm 39.6.
correction_note: Title, full author list (Sanakoyeu, Khalidov, McCarthy, Vedaldi, Neverova), venue CVPR 2020 and arXiv ID 2003.00080 are all CONFIRMED — verified from the first author's own repo README (github.com/asanakoy/densepose-evolution), which states the byline and links arxiv.org/pdf/2003.00080.pdf. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE INPUT RECORD. (1) The dataset numbers were mislabeled. The record said 'DensePose-Chimps (500 train / 430 test annotated correspondences)'. Those are INSTANCE counts for the CSE splits, not correspondence counts: 500 instances / 350 images train, 430 instances / 304 images val, with ~3 point correspondences per instance. The chart-based DensePose-Chimps set is separately 930 instances / 654 images and is validation-only. (2) The code_url is misleading. github.com/asanakoy/densepose-evolution contains no code and no LICENSE file at all (root = docs/ + README.md; /blob/master/LICENSE is a 404); the README itself redirects to detectron2, where the method actually ships under Apache-2.0. Anyone told to 'clone the repo' will get nothing. NOTE ON VERIFICATION METHOD: arxiv.org, openaccess.thecvf.com, dblp.org, api.crossref.org, api.openalex.org, api.semanticscholar.org, ieeexplore.ieee.org and huggingface.co are ALL blocked by this session's network egress proxy, and the session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was already exhausted before I started. I verified entirely through github.com, which is reachable: the author's own repo README, detectron2's DENSEPOSE_DATASETS.md, DENSEPOSE_CSE.md, the chimps finetune YAML, densepose/data/meshes/builtin.py, and detectron2's LICENSE. That is an official/author-controlled primary source but not the arXiv abs page or publisher page.

citation: Remy Sabathier, Niloy J. Mitra, David Novotny. "Animal Avatars: Reconstructing Animatable 3D Animals from Casual Videos." In Computer Vision - ECCV 2024, LNCS, Part LXXIX, pp. 270-287. Springer, 2024. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-031-72986-7_16. arXiv:2403.17103. Selected as an Oral at ECCV 2024.
license: CC-BY-NC-4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International) — VERIFIED by fetching and reading LICENSE.txt in the repo. NON-COMMERCIAL ONLY; Section 2(a)(1) restricts use to NonCommercial purposes. DEPENDENCY LICENSE IS WORSE AND IS THE REAL BLOCKER: the pipeline requires the SMAL dog model from BITE (github.com/runa91/bite_release), which I also fetched — it ships under a custom MPI 'Software Copyright License for non-commercial scientific research purposes', a click-through EULA binding on clone, with commercial licensing routed to ps-licensing@tue.mpg.de. So the whole stack is research-only via two independent restrictions.
representation_3d: SMAL parametric template (the BITE/BARC dog variant) + Continuous Surface Embeddings for dense image-to-mesh correspondence, plus an implicit duplex-mesh TEXTURE defined in the CANONICAL POSE and deformed to each frame by the SMAL pose coefficients. This canonical-pose appearance model is precisely the 'identity pattern in a pose-free space' construct the sevengill question is asking about — but it is built for novel-view rendering and animation, never evaluated for identity matching.
species_domain: Dogs. Uses the BITE dog SMAL basis (my_smpl_39dogsnorm_newv3_dog.pkl + symmetry indices) and the DensePose-RCNN soft-animals CSE weights; evaluated on the CoP3D casual-video dataset.
supervision: Monocular casual video only. No 3D ground truth, no multi-view rig, no per-frame manual keypoints. Off-the-shelf preprocessing supplies everything: Segment-Anything for masks, RAFT for optical flow, VGGSfM for cameras, DensePose CSE for dense correspondences.
data_requirement: NOT STATED in the repo README, which I fetched: no frame count per sequence, no GPU model, no per-sequence optimization time, no memory figure. What IS stated is the dependency manifest, which is the honest cost estimate — per sequence you need a monocular video plus SAM masks, RAFT flow, VGGSfM camera poses, and DensePose CSE maps, and up front you need (a) a species SMAL-style shape basis and (b) a species CSE model. For a subset of CoP3D scenes the authors ship precomputed refined masks, init shape and sparse per-frame keypoints in external_data/, which implies the raw off-the-shelf preprocessing was not reliable enough on its own. I could not fetch the paper itself for the numeric ablations — arxiv.org is egress-blocked in this session and the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so frames/GPU-hours remain unverified rather than absent.
elongate_relevance: low as a transferable method, high as a proof-of-concept for the idea. The recipe (CSE correspondences + canonical-pose texture from casual monocular video) is exactly the technical core the sevengill proposal needs, and it demonstrates the idea works end-to-end. But the deformation model is linear blend skinning over a rigid-limbed quadruped skeleton with a fixed SMAL shape basis; large-amplitude anguilliform axial undulation, which is the dominant deformation mode of a Notorynchus trunk, is outside that model. It also inherits both missing prerequisites: there is no SMAL-analogous shape basis and no CSE model for any elasmobranch. Note the asker already has half of prerequisite (a) — SharkSMPL is a working SMPL-analogous parametric shark model — but it is a 16-joint LAMNIFORM template built on a great white with five gill slits and two dorsals, so it does not transfer to a hexanchiform without a new template mesh, a re-rooted kinematic tree with more axial joints for lateral bending, and a landmark schema that drops second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip and relocates the single dorsal posteriorly near the pelvics.
key_numbers: ECCV 2024 Oral; LNCS Part LXXIX pp. 270-287; DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-72986-7_16. Quantitative results not retrievable (arXiv blocked).

citation: Francis Williams, Alexander Bock, Harish Doraiswamy, Cassandra Donatelli, Kayla Hall, Adam Summers, Daniele Panozzo, Claudio T. Silva. "Unwind: Interactive Fish Straightening." arXiv:1904.04890, 2019 (rev. 2020). VENUE UNCONFIRMED - do not assert a venue in the final report.
venue: UNCONFIRMED - not a verified conference or journal; cite as arXiv preprint until checked
confidence_note: code and license VERIFIED by fetch; bibliographic venue still unverifiable
license: none found - VERIFIED. No LICENSE file appears in the repository root listing, and raw.githubusercontent.com/fwilliams/unwind/{master,main}/LICENSE both return HTTP 404. GitHub reports no license in the sidebar. TREAT AS ALL RIGHTS RESERVED - no right to copy, modify, or redistribute. Contact the authors (Panozzo / Silva, NYU) before any reuse.
representation_3d: Volumetric (CT) straightening: interactively extracts, UNBENDS and UNTWISTS a bent fish specimen inside a 3D volume, computing a deformation into a straight canonical frame. Genuinely a 3D canonicalisation - but of a static CT volume, not of image-space appearance. CORRECTION TO FORM: this is a compiled C++/Qt5 DESKTOP GUI APPLICATION, not a Python library - it needs a C++14 compiler, CMake 3.8+, Qt5, Xorg dev libraries, Boost, MPFR, GMP, and vcpkg on Windows. It does NOT unwrap to UV and builds no canonical surface — it studies viewpoint sensitivity empirically. So it is NOT a canonical-3D-surface-mapping paper; it is the control experiment you run before deciding whether you need one.

Splits: train 64,000 images (top-only or side-only) / 128,000 (topside); test 16,000 images per query and per gallery for top and side, 32,000 for topside. Three evaluation protocols shipped: top->side, side->top, topside->topside. Packaged as data.hdf5 + metadata.json; unpack script pack.py; FastReID-compatible dataloader MOO.py provided. NOTE: the record's headline scientific claims — that asymmetric coat patterns make identity strongly viewpoint-sensitive, and that there is a 'critical elevation threshold' above which models generalise to unseen views — are NOT verifiable from any source I could reach. They may well be correct; treat them as unconfirmed until someone reads the PDF.
elongate_relevance: low — cattle, and it builds no canonical surface, so nothing about hexanchid geometry is addressed. Its value to the sevengill question is methodological, not zoological: it is a cheap, template-free way to ask 'how much of my re-ID error is just viewpoint?' before spending months on a 3D template. That question is MORE acute for a sevengill than for cattle, because a laterally-bending anguilliform trunk with a single posterior dorsal presents a far wider range of apparent silhouettes than a rigid quadruped, and the lab's 661GB corpus is certainly not uniformly sampled in viewpoint. The transferable recipe — render a textured mesh in Blender across a dense viewpoint grid, measure where re-ID breaks, then transfer — is species-agnostic and the lab already owns the Blender domain-randomisation machinery from shark-pose-3d. Caveat: the whole design assumes a rigid body under viewpoint change, and a sevengill's identity-bearing flank deforms non-rigidly, which MOO's protocol cannot represent.

species_domain: Grevy's zebra (Equus grevyi). Quadruped, rigid barrel torso.
representation_3d: Explicit-template route. SMALST fits the SMAL (horse/zebra) parametric mesh — 3D pose + shape + texture — to a single monocular image; the coat is back-projected onto the fitted surface, yielding a viewpoint- and pose-normalised UV TEXTURE MAP. A CROP of that atlas (hindquarter + back only, NOT the full atlas) is then fed to deep metric learning (ResNet, softmax + reciprocal triplet loss) and matched by kNN in the learned embedding. Pre-stages: MegaDetector v4.1 animal detection at confidence threshold 0.83 (AUC-optimised) with padded boxes, then Microsoft AI4Earth SpeciesClassification for species disambiguation.
supervision: No per-image UV annotation. Uses the pretrained SMALST regressor (itself trained on synthetic textured zebra renders plus real images with masks/keypoints) off the shelf; the only new supervision is individual identity labels for the metric-learning head. Note: left and right flanks are treated as SEPARATE identity classes — the repo states explicitly 'Each side of the animal has a distinctive pattern so must be classified separately.'
data_requirement: VERY SMALL, and this is the load-bearing caveat. Identity dataset = the SMALST test + validation splits combined: 4 unique images of each of 37 individual Grevy's zebras (~148 images total), from The Great Grevy's Rally 2018. So ~4 images per individual, SINGLE VIEW per image, no multi-view rig. Image resolution: not stated. GPU-hours: not stated (compute credited to the University of Bristol ACRC). Trained weights are NOT released — the repo lists both 'deep 3D fitting model - to be added soon' and 'deep metric learning model - to be added soon', and the last push was 2022-08-30, so the pipeline is not reproducible out of the box. The authors' own README calls the study 'far too small to estimate the full performance potential… acts as a proof-of-concept'.
key_numbers: 56.8% individual identification accuracy on the SMALST dataset (VERIFIED verbatim in the authors' README). The 48.0% 2D-baseline figure asserted in the input record could NOT be verified — it does not appear in the repo and arXiv is unreachable from this session; treat 48.0% as UNVERIFIED. Detector threshold 0.83. 37 individuals × 4 images.
elongate_relevance: low — quadruped with a rigid barrel torso, i.e. the easy case for a fixed UV atlas; a laterally-bending anguilliform sevengill trunk is the hard case this paper never tests. But its ARCHITECTURAL relevance is high: it is the bolt-on version of the hypothesis (back-project to UV, then metric-learn) that maps directly onto the lab's existing SharkSMPL asset (template + kinematic tree + LBS + keypoint regressor already exist; only the back-projection-to-UV step is missing). Two transferable warnings: (a) they had to CROP to specific body regions rather than use the whole atlas, implying UV regions with poor fit or heavy foreshortening actively hurt — for a sevengill that likely means the elongate caudal upper lobe and the broad blunt head are exclusion zones; (b) UV normalisation did NOT unify left and right flanks, so a sevengill catalogue would still be doubled and the space is not truly pose-free.

elongate_relevance: low — quadruped, and the SMAL shape space is a quadruped shape space that cannot represent a sevengill at all. But the METHOD is body-plan agnostic in one specific, valuable way: the uv-flow texture head needs only a template carrying a UV atlas, which a sevengill template would have to supply. The trick worth stealing is exactly the one the record identifies: predicting WHERE each texel samples from, rather than predicting texture RGB, means the model cannot hallucinate pattern. For pigmentation-based ID that is the difference between a hole (recoverable, you just get no vote from that region) and an invented spot (poisons the match). It also validates the lab's existing synthetic-render-then-domain-transfer strategy from shark-pose-3d. Caveat for a sevengill: uv-flow assumes the fit is good enough that the sampled pixel really is that surface point; on a laterally-bending trunk a small pose error slides the sample along the flank, which is precisely where the speckle pattern lives.

species_domain: Humans, chimpanzees, and 9 LVIS animal categories (bear, cow, cat, dog, elephant, giraffe, horse, sheep, zebra). ALL MAMMALS. I enumerated the complete registered mesh catalogue from source (builtin.py): smpl_27554, chimp_5029, cat_5001, cat_7466, dog_5002, dog_7466, sheep_5004, zebra_5002, horse_5004, giraffe_5002, elephant_5002, cow_5002, bear_4936 — 13 meshes, zero fish, zero elasmobranchs, zero limbless or elongate taxa. Mesh vertex counts are encoded in the names, so chimp_5029 = 5,029 verts, comparable in scale to SharkSMPL's 3,912-vert template.
representation_3d: Learns a per-pixel embedding of the CORRESPONDING MESH VERTEX rather than a chart-based (I,u,v) parameterisation, so there are no chart seams. Architecture (from DENSEPOSE_CSE.md): Faster R-CNN + FPN; per detected object the model predicts coarse segmentation S (2 channels, fg/bg) and an embedding E of 16 CHANNELS; a separate embedder produces vertex embeddings Ê for the mesh; E and Ê are matched to derive each pixel's surface position. Requires a canonical 3D mesh per category, plus precomputed geodesic distances, symmetry and texcoords per mesh (all four files per entry in the catalogue).
supervision: Extremely sparse manual point-to-vertex correspondences plus foreground masks — annotation type dp_x, dp_y, dp_vertex, ref_model. Far cheaper than DensePose's full IUV annotation. Also supports class-agnostic (CA) training, where all annotated instances map to a single category, and cross-category transfer.

Verified from projects/DensePose/doc/DENSEPOSE_DATASETS.md: DensePose-Chimps CSE — TRAIN 500 INSTANCES across 350 IMAGES; VAL 430 INSTANCES across 304 IMAGES; at ~3 point-to-vertex correspondences PER INSTANCE (so ~1,500 train correspondences, ~1,290 val). DensePose-LVIS CSE ds1 (the split used in this paper) — train 4,141 images / 9,472 segmentations / 5,184 DensePose annotations over the 9 animal categories; val 571 / 1,537 / 1,036. ds2 (the 2021 follow-up) — train 13,746 images / 46,964 segms / 18,932 DP annots on selected animals; val 2,690 / 9,155 / 3,604. Human CSE pretraining uses DensePose-COCO CSE: 39,210 instances / 26,437 images (train2014) + 7,297 / 5,984 (valminusminival). VIEWS: single monocular image, no multi-view. RESOLUTION: annotation points are normalised to a 256x256 bounding box; masks are 256x256 RLE. COMPUTE, from the model zoo tables: human CSE R_50_FPN_s1x = 0.349 s/iter, 6.3 GB train mem, 0.060 s/im inference. Species transfer is a SHORT FINETUNE, not a retrain: R_50_FPN_soft_chimps_finetune_4k = 4,000 iterations at 0.569 s/iter and 4.7 GB (roughly 40 min on one GPU), reaching dp.AP GPS 32.2 / GPSm 39.6. The 9-animal finetune R_50_FPN_soft_animals_finetune_4k = 4K iters, 0.381 s/iter, 7.3 GB, dp.AP GPS 21.3 (class-agnostic variant 25.4).
key_numbers: 16-channel embedding. Human CSE dp.AP GPS 64.4 (R_50_FPN_s1x) / 65.5 (R_50_FPN_DL_s1x). Chimp transfer via 4K-iteration finetune: dp.AP GPS 32.2. Nine-quadruped transfer: dp.AP GPS 21.3 (CA 25.4). Chimps annotation budget 500 train instances / 350 images at ~3 clicks each. 13 registered meshes, all mammalian.
elongate_relevance: low, and this is a real, source-verified gap rather than an impression. I enumerated the entire released CSE mesh catalogue from builtin.py: every one of the 13 meshes is a mammal (human SMPL + 11 primate/quadruped). There is NO fish, elasmobranch, snake, eel or other elongate/limbless reference mesh in any released CSE model or dataset. A sevengill CSE would be the first of its kind for that body plan. That said, CSE is still the RIGHT primitive for this problem and clearly better than DensePose charts: because it embeds vertices directly instead of carving the surface into charts, there are no seams to fall arbitrarily along a sevengill's flank — exactly where the speckle and scar signal lives. Two hard cautions from the verified numbers. (1) The mesh is the blocker: the lab has a great white template, and a sevengill differs in precisely the topology-relevant ways (single posterior dorsal vs two, seven gill slits vs five, elongate anguilliform trunk, very long caudal upper lobe) — the 16-keypoint white-shark schema does not transfer, and neither does the template. (2) The transfer numbers degrade sharply with phylogenetic distance from the pretraining manifold: chimps (near-human) reach dp.AP GPS 32.2, but nine ordinary quadrupeds only 21.3. An elasmobranch is vastly further from the human/quadruped manifold than any of those, so expect the human-CSE-pretrain-then-finetune shortcut to yield much less than 21.3, or to require training the embedder largely from scratch. FEASIBILITY UPSIDE: 500 instances at ~3 clicks each is the same order as the lab's existing 689-image keypoint effort in shark-morphometrics, and SharkScarAnnotator (SAM2 segmentation, 12 body zones, consensus) is already most of the annotation tool needed.

Original facebookresearch/DensePose repo = CC-BY-NC 4.0 — VERIFIED by fetching the raw LICENSE, which opens 'Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International'. NON-COMMERCIAL. The successor implementation inside detectron2 is Apache-2.0 — VERIFIED separately (see cse-2020). Separately, the DensePose-COCO annotations are distributed from dl.fbaipublicfiles.com and inherit COCO image licensing, which is per-image Flickr terms — not resolvable from this session.
species_domain: Humans only.
representation_3d: SMPL mesh (6,890 verts) cut into 24 body-part CHARTS, each with its own 2D (u,v) atlas normalised to [0,1]. Output per foreground pixel = (part index I, u, v). A coarser 14-part segmentation is used for masks: Torso, Right Hand, Left Hand, Left Foot, Right Foot, Upper Leg R/L, Lower Leg R/L, Upper Arm L/R, Lower Arm L/R, Head. Note the modern CSE mesh catalogue registers a subdivided smpl_27554 (27,554 verts) for the embedding-based successor.
supervision: Fully manual dense annotation. Annotators first paint the body part, then click the corresponding point on a rendered 3D part surface — a two-stage per-point protocol. Point annotations are dp_x, dp_y (image coords relative to the box, normalised to 256x256), dp_I (fine chart index), dp_U, dp_V (chart coords); masks are dp_masks, RLE at 256x256.
data_requirement: ALL VERIFIED VERBATIM from projects/DensePose/doc/DENSEPOSE_DATASETS.md. DensePose-COCO contains about 50K annotated persons. Splits: densepose_train2014 = 39,210 instances / 26,437 images (526 MB); densepose_valminusminival2014 = 7,297 instances / 5,984 images (105 MB); densepose_minival2014 = 2,243 instances / 1,508 images (31 MB). Train uses train2014 + valminusminival2014; minival2014 is validation. Annotation density: ~100 hand-clicked points per annotated instance, plus the 14-part coarse mask. DensePose-PoseTrack adds 8,274 instances / 1,680 images / 36 tracks (train) and 4,753 / 782 / 46 (val), also at ~100 points per instance. VIEWS: single monocular image; no multi-view. RESOLUTION: annotations normalised to a 256x256 bounding-box frame; source images are COCO train2014/val2014. GPU-HOURS for the original 2018 training: not stated in the repo (the detectron2 legacy model-zoo tables give per-iteration times for the reimplementation, not the original run).
key_numbers: ~50K annotated persons; ~100 clicked pixel-to-surface correspondences per instance; 39,210 / 7,297 / 2,243 instances across 26,437 / 5,984 / 1,508 images; 24 fine charts; 14 coarse parts; SMPL 6,890 verts.
elongate_relevance: low, and cautionary — this is the formulation to LEARN FROM and then NOT ADOPT. Two independent reasons. (1) Cost: ~100 hand-clicked pixel-to-surface correspondences per instance is roughly 33x the per-instance annotation burden of the CSE route (~3 clicks), and any shark version starting from the chart formulation inherits that burden wholesale. Against the lab's 689 annotated images in shark-morphometrics, chart-style DensePose annotation would be a multi-month effort; CSE-style would be days. (2) Topology: the 24-chart atlas is carved along human LIMB topology, with seams deliberately placed at joints so they fall on low-information creases. A sevengill has no limbs and therefore no analogous natural chart boundaries — its trunk is one continuous laterally-flexing tube. Chart seams would land arbitrarily along the flank, which is exactly where the speckle/spot pigmentation and the scar signal live, so the chart primitive would introduce discontinuities straight through the identity signature. The chart formulation is the wrong primitive for this body plan; CSE is the one to adopt. Historically indispensable as the origin of the 'map every pixel to a fixed (u,v) on a canonical template' idea the research question is built on.

species_domain: Category-level animal/object shapes. Repo ships models for 'bird' (CUB-200-2011) and 'horse' (Pascal), plus a models.zip covering additional ImageNet categories. The sibling CSM README states this follow-up work 'show[s] results on over 10 categories' (verified quote from the official csm README). All released categories are tetrapods (quadrupeds + birds). NO fish, NO elongate/anguilliform body plan.
representation_3d: Per-pixel mapping from image to a point on a CANONICAL 3D TEMPLATE SURFACE, predicted jointly with camera pose and per-part articulation. The template is decomposed into soft parts arranged in a hand-authored hierarchy. VERIFIED from docs/setup.md: every released category ships a base template shape (model.obj), a mean_shape.mat carrying UV-to-face mappings, kp2vertex.txt, a part hierarchy definition (hierarchy.xml), and mirror_transforms.txt for articulation correspondence.
supervision: CORRECTION TO THE INPUT RECORD. The paper's headline claim is training from foreground masks only, and I have no reason to doubt it, but I could NOT fetch the abstract to quote it (arxiv.org blocked). What I CAN verify from docs/setup.md is more nuanced: the repo says 'Keypoint annotations (optional - models can train with or without them)' and ships part segmentation configs of 3, 8, or 0 parts. So keypoint-free training is a supported configuration, not the only one, and the released checkpoints are not all mask-only. Separately, the input record's phrase 'no correspondence annotation' is right, but it understates the asset burden: a per-category template mesh AND a hand-authored part hierarchy (hierarchy.xml) AND mirror_transforms.txt must be supplied by hand. For a sevengill that is bespoke authoring work, not a free lunch.
data_requirement: Images per individual: N/A - this is a CATEGORY-level correspondence method, not an individual-level one. It needs no repeat sightings of the same animal and provides no identity signal on its own. Views: monocular, single image, no multi-view rig. Training set size, image resolution, GPU count, batch size, epochs and GPU-hours: NOT STATED in the repo (docs/setup.md and the README give none; the paper itself was unreachable). Only concrete compute facts I could verify: Python 2.7, PyTorch 1.2.0/1.3.0, CUDA 9.2, and the repo generates SLURM scripts (implying a multi-GPU cluster job, but no count is given). Data actually required: an image collection with foreground masks + a category template mesh + part hierarchy.
key_numbers: CVPR 2020 pp. 452-461. 'over 10 categories' per the authors' own csm README. Part decompositions of 0/3/8 parts. No PCK/correspondence numbers verified - the paper PDF was unreachable, so I am reporting NO accuracy metrics rather than inventing them.
elongate_relevance: medium-high - the soft-part-decomposition plus learned-articulation formulation is the least body-plan-committed machinery in this cluster and would let you place many short segments along an undulating trunk instead of a limb-shaped kinematic tree, but the part hierarchy is HAND-AUTHORED per template, so nothing is discovered for free, and I found zero evidence anyone has run ACSM on a non-tetrapod. Also note that the 16-keypoint white-shark schema is irrelevant here in the mask-only configuration, which is actually an advantage given that schema does not transfer to a sevengill (no second dorsal, posterior single dorsal, seven gill slits).

representation_3d: Category-level 3D template mesh; the network predicts, per foreground pixel, a point on that template plus a camera, trained by a geometric cycle-consistency loss (reproject the predicted 3D template point and require it to land back on the originating pixel).
supervision: Foreground masks + a category template mesh, with no dense correspondence annotation and no keypoint supervision in the headline setting. I could NOT fetch the paper to quote the exact supervision statement (arxiv.org and thecvf.com both blocked). elongate_relevance: low-medium - supervision is cheap enough that SharkScarAnnotator's SAM2 masks would satisfy it, but geometric cycle consistency degenerates on surfaces with low geometric distinctiveness, and a smooth, near-cylindrical, laterally-flexing shark flank is close to the worst case: many template points reproject to near-identical pixels, so the cycle loss is weakly constraining exactly along the anterior-posterior axis where you most need correspondence to be sharp for scar/pigment matching. Also CSM as published is the non-articulated formulation; a sevengill's lateral undulation is precisely what it does not model. Prefer ACSM over CSM on both licensing and articulation grounds.

Do not put scan counts, vertex counts, or shape-component counts in the final report unless someone fetches the primary source; I am deliberately not supplying numbers I did not read. What IS verified, from the downstream smalst repo: it requires the MPI SMPL model download plus Google-Drive-hosted train/test/val sets, with test and validation images drawn from The Great Grevy's Rally 2018 zebra census. No GPU-hours, resolution, or image counts are stated in that repo either. Images per individual: N/A for SMAL itself (category shape model, not re-ID).

elongate_relevance: low - and the finding is a strong NEGATIVE that should be stated plainly in the report. SMAL and every descendant (SMALR, SMALST, BARC, BITE, RAC, 3D-Fauna, Animal Avatars) is a QUADRUPED model: the mesh topology, the limb-structured kinematic tree, and the PCA shape space are all wrong for a hexanchiform, and none of it is extensible to a fish by fitting. Concretely for this project: the great-white SharkSMPL template is ALSO wrong for a sevengill - one dorsal not two (so first_dorsal_base/tip and second_dorsal_base/tip in the 16-keypoint schema collapse to a single posteriorly-placed dorsal pair, and two of the sixteen canonical keypoints have no anatomical referent at all), the dorsal sits far posterior near the pelvics rather than mid-body, there are seven gill slits not five (gill_slit as a single keypoint is already lossy and becomes more so), the upper caudal lobe is much longer, and a 16-joint white-shark tree will badly under-articulate a laterally-flexible anguilliform trunk. The 'just retarget SharkSMPL' shortcut is not available; a sevengill needs the bespoke template + kinematic tree + shape space effort done again from scratch.

citation: Thomas J. Cashman, Andrew W. Fitzgibbon. "What Shape Are Dolphins? Building 3D Morphable Models from 2D Images." IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 2013 (IEEE Xplore document 6165306; first published online 2012). NOTE: the 'ECCV 2012' half of the input citation is UNSUPPORTED — see correction_note. Volume/issue/page numbers deliberately omitted because I could not verify them.
venue: IEEE TPAMI (IEEE Xplore doc 6165306). The claimed ECCV 2012 venue could not be substantiated.
license: Microsoft Public License (Ms-PL) — VERIFIED by fetching https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmmanley/forms/master/LICENSE.md. Permissive, OSI-approved, COMMERCIAL USE PERMITTED. Grants a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free copyright license to reproduce and prepare derivative works, plus a patent license; conditions are attribution-notice retention, a patent-retaliation clause, and that source redistributions carry the full license. NO non-commercial restriction, NO registration, NO EULA. This makes it one of the very few 3D-animal-morphable-model codebases in this whole scan that is NOT research-only — a sharp contrast with SMPL/SMAL/SMALST (registration + non-commercial) and with NORPPA (custom non-commercial).
species_domain: Dolphins (32 instances), plus bananas, pigeons and bears as the other shipped projects. Smooth, limbless, streamlined aquatic body built from ordinary 2D photographs.
representation_3d: A 3D morphable model represented as a LINEAR COMBINATION OF SUBDIVISION SURFACES, initialised from a single coarse rigid template control mesh and fitted to a collection of 2D silhouettes with surface-normal noise modelling. Deformation is continuous surface deformation of the subdivision control cage, NOT a joint tree and NOT linear blend skinning — a real architectural difference from SharkSMPL, and arguably a better fit for a body that bends continuously along its axis rather than at discrete joints. It produces GEOMETRY ONLY: no texture, no UV atlas, no dense surface correspondence for appearance, no identity.
supervision: 2D silhouettes only — no 3D scans anywhere in the pipeline. The shipped dolphin dataset uses MANUAL segmentations; the paper's original results used GrabCut silhouettes from PowerPoint 2010, and the README states there is 'no significant difference between the manual and automatic segmentations; the results are very similar'. Camera translation and scale per image are recovered automatically by the provided align_project function rather than hand-annotated.
data_requirement: VERIFIED FROM THE OFFICIAL README, and unusually cheap: the dolphin model is built from 32 DOLPHIN INSTANCES, ONE VIEW EACH (a collection of independent single-view photographs of different animals, not multi-view capture of one animal), fitted with 8 basis shapes: forms(dolphins, 8, 0.5, 0.25, 10). Comparators in the same release: bananas 2 basis shapes; pigeons 7 basis shapes (align_project then forms(pigeons, 7, 0.25, 0.05, 5)); bears 10 basis shapes (0.25, 0.25, 4). The sigma_norm parameter is 10 for the shipped manual segmentations versus 40/3 in the paper, because manual segmentations give more reliable normals. Compute: CPU only, MATLAB R2017a plus the Optimization Toolbox; NO GPU, NO GPU-hours reported. Runtime is not quantified but the README explicitly warns 'you should expect some of these optimizations to take a long time', singling out the dolphins project as the slowest. Image resolution: not stated.
key_numbers: 32 dolphin instances, 8 basis shapes, single view per instance, 0 3D scans, 0 GPUs. That combination is the headline result for the lab: a usable 3D morphable model of a limbless swimmer from three dozen ordinary single-view photos.
elongate_relevance: medium-high — right body plan (limbless streamlined swimmer) and it is the strongest published rebuttal to 'a new-species parametric model needs a scan campaign', which matters because the lab's SharkSMPL rests on a single DigitalLife3D great-white mesh; but it is geometry-only with no texture/UV/identity, subdivision surfaces rather than a kinematic tree, and 2012-era MATLAB, so it is a design precedent and a licensing outlier rather than a build target.
correction_note: PAPER EXISTENCE: WELL SUPPORTED. VENUE: PARTLY CORRECTED. I verified the work through its official code release, which reproduces Cashman and Fitzgibbon's own documentation verbatim ('Forms: Flexible Object Reconstruction from Multiple Silhouettes — Thomas J. Cashman, University of Lugano; Andrew W. Fitzgibbon, Microsoft Research, Cambridge. This MATLAB code gives the implementation for our paper "What Shape are Dolphins? Building 3D Morphable Models from 2D Images"'). The repo is a 2018 update by Jason M. Manley (Rockefeller University, jmanley@rockefeller.edu) of source 'retrieved from https://archive.codeplex.com/?p=forms', i.e. Fitzgibbon's original Microsoft CodePlex release — which also explains the Ms-PL. CORRECTION 1: the repository points to the paper as http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6165306/, i.e. the IEEE TPAMI version. I found NO evidence for an ECCV 2012 paper of this title and I would drop that half of the citation. Residual uncertainty is real, though: ieeexplore.ieee.org, doi.org, api.crossref.org, dblp.org and every other bibliographic host are blocked in this session and WebSearch was exhausted (200/200), so 'found no evidence' here means 'could not look', not 'checked and absent'. A human should confirm the venue line before publication. CORRECTION 2: I deliberately did NOT write volume 35, issue 1, pages 232-244 or a DOI into the citation, even though the input record asserted 35(1) 2013 — I could not verify those and inventing plausible page numbers is exactly the failure mode to avoid. CORRECTION 3: the authors capitalise the title 'What Shape are Dolphins?' (lowercase 'are') in their own README; IEEE renders it 'What Shape Are Dolphins?'. Minor, but note the discrepancy. CORRECTION 4 — THE BIGGEST FIX: the input record said code_url 'NOT FOUND' and license 'unknown'. BOTH ARE WRONG. Working code exists at github.com/jmmanley/forms (MATLAB, 7 stars, 3 forks, topics 3d-models/3d-reconstruction/dolphin/morphable-model/silhouette-reconstruction, last updated 2022-04-07) and it is Ms-PL. It ships runnable projects including the 32-instance dolphin dataset with manual segmentations, and the 2018 update added GUI tools, restructured output, and — notably for a re-ID use case — the ability to FIT THE LEARNED MODEL TO IMAGES OUTSIDE THE ORIGINAL TRAINING SET. The input record's characterisation of this paper as 'historical context rather than a build target' is therefore too dismissive: it is the only permissively-licensed, actually-downloadable aquatic morphable-model code in the scan.
supervision_note: Silhouette-only supervision is verified from the authors' own README, not inferred.

supervision: Very cheap, and this part is VERIFIED from IPanda_get_kp.ipynb: 3 source keypoints are manually clicked on ONE reference image, then propagated to the entire dataset by matching DIFT features (Stable Diffusion 2.1, prompt-conditioned) at diffusion timesteps t=0 and t=261, ensemble size 8, 1280-channel features, 14x14 spatial maps upsampled to 100x100, nearest-neighbour by cosine similarity. data_requirement: VERIFIED FROM THE NOTEBOOKS (the paper itself was unreadable). Dataset: iPanda-50 split disjoint-by-class into 5,266 training / 1,286 database (gallery) / 322 query images. GPU-hours: not stated anywhere.
elongate_relevance: high — body-plan agnostic by construction, since the keypoint set is a free parameter and the landmark-category embedding is what lets a schema be swapped without retraining a hard-coded ordering. This is precisely the property the lab's 16-keypoint white-shark Schema v2 lacks, and it matters because that schema does NOT transfer to Notorynchus cepedianus: second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip have no referent (sevengills have a single dorsal), first_dorsal sits far posterior near the pelvics rather than mid-body, the single gill_slit landmark under-describes seven slits, and an anguilliform laterally-flexing trunk arguably needs extra mid-trunk landmarks that the white-shark schema never needed. It also plugs directly into assets the lab already owns (the trained YOLOv8n-pose detector, 689 train / 163 val images).

venue: IEEE TPAMI (one index lists it as TPAMI 2025, another as TPAMI 2024 - the arXiv posting is April 2024)
code_url: https://github.com/YvanYin/Metric3D (project page: https://jugghm.github.io/Metric3Dv2/ , blocked this session)
license: BSD-2-Clause. README section 'License and Contact' states 'The Metric 3D code is under a 2-clause BSD License.' PERMISSIVE, COMMERCIALLY USABLE - this is the good case, unlike the SMAL/SMPL-derived and MegaDescriptor-L items elsewhere in this scan. TWO CAVEATS: (a) the README adds 'For further commercial inquiries, please contact Dr. Wei Yin and Mr. Mu Hu', which sits oddly beside BSD-2 and may indicate the authors consider the WEIGHTS separately licensed - no separate weights licence is stated anywhere in the repo, checkpoints are served from Google Drive and HuggingFace with no licence file; (b) the v2 backbone is DINOv2-with-registers, and I verified facebookresearch/dinov2 is Apache-2.0, so the backbone lineage is clean.
species_domain: General terrestrial natural imagery. NOT marine, NOT underwater, no animal-specific training. The README's own Q&A warns: 'metric 3D is not almighty. Some objects (chandeliers, drones...) / camera views (aerial view, bev...) do not occur frequently in the training datasets.'
representation_3d: Zero-shot monocular METRIC depth plus surface normals. Canonical-camera-space formulation. Architecture: DINOv2-reg ViT-Small / ViT-Large / ViT-giant2 encoder with a RAFT-style iterative decoder (4 iterations for S, 8 for L and g). ONNX exports exist for all three sizes.
supervision: None at inference - frozen foundation model. BUT NOT ACTUALLY ZERO-CONFIG: it needs camera intrinsics. README: the canonical camera is img_size=(512, 960) with focal_length=1000.0, cx/cy at half image size; inference resizes to crop_size=(512, 1088); in the wild-mode script, 'as no intrinsics are provided, we provided by default 9 settings of focal length', and the README's Q1 is literally 'Why depth maps look good but pointclouds are distorted? Because the focal length is not properly set!'
data_requirement: From the repo README benchmark tables: pretrain + train = '142M + 16M' (142M-image backbone pretraining inherited from the DINOv2 lineage, plus ~16M labelled depth training images) - compare DepthAnything at 142M + 63M and OmniData v2 at 1.3M + 12.2M. Released checkpoint filename 'metric_depth_vit_giant2_800k.pth' implies 800k training iterations. Working resolution 512x960 canonical / 512x1088 inference crop. GPU-hours: NOT STATED in the README; I could not read the paper (arXiv blocked) so a per-GPU-hour figure may exist there. Images-per-individual and view count are not applicable - it is single-image, no per-subject data requirement.
key_numbers: Verified from the repo README. Metric depth, fine-tuned: KITTI AbsRel 0.044 / d1 0.985 (ViT-L), 0.039 / 0.989 (ViT-giant2); NYU AbsRel 0.047 / d1 0.989 (ViT-L). Affine-invariant zero-shot (ViT-L): KITTI AbsRel 0.042, NYUv2 0.042, DIODE-Full 0.141, ETH3D 0.042. SURFACE NORMALS - the part that actually matters for a UV-unwrapping pipeline (ViT-L): NYU 11.25deg accuracy 0.688, mean angular error 12.0deg, RMS 19.2; ScanNet 11.25deg 0.760, mean 9.9deg; iBims 11.25deg 0.694, mean 19.4deg. Claimed SOTA on 10+ depth and normal benchmarks; won the 2nd Monocular Depth Estimation Challenge at CVPR 2023 (v1).
elongate_relevance: high (as a risk item, not as a method). It is the load-bearing off-the-shelf dependency of the pelage-unwrapping seed method, and it is the component most likely to fail on a turbid-water elongate subject. Three concrete failure vectors now backed by repo evidence rather than speculation: (1) TRAINING DISTRIBUTION is terrestrial indoor/outdoor scenes - the 11.25deg normal numbers above are all from NYU/ScanNet/iBims, i.e. furnished rooms, and the README explicitly concedes degradation on camera views under-represented in training; (2) INTRINSICS - the model needs a focal length, and the lab's 661GB corpus spans 4 sites and 14 years of mixed cameras in underwater housings, where dome/flat-port refraction changes the effective focal length; a wrong focal silently distorts the reconstruction (README Q1); (3) the seed method feeds it the ORIGINAL IMAGE WITH BACKGROUND on purpose, and here that background is green water, backscatter and kelp rather than ground planes and horizons. The candidate record's proposed one-day experiment is the right call and I would sharpen it: run the ViT-L and ViT-giant2 checkpoints on a few dozen sevengill and white-shark frames, sweep the 9 default focal settings, and inspect the NORMAL maps (not the depth maps) along the flank - if the normals do not track the body's lateral curvature the seed pipeline has no foundation and the lab should fall back to a template/CSE route or stay 2D. Note also that for a sevengill specifically, the failure would be worst exactly where the identity signal lives: the elongate, laterally-bending trunk whose curvature is the thing the normals must resolve.

The bootstrap works because chimp and human share a limbed body plan and (in the chart-based version) can borrow the human chart atlas outright. There is NO existing source model anywhere in this lineage that is proximal to a hexanchiform shark, so for a sevengill the trick has no donor: a mammalian source cannot supply charts for a limbless, anguilliform, single-posterior-dorsal body with seven gill slits and a long-upper-lobe heterocercal caudal. The correct reading for this lab is that the DONOR must be built in-house - the SharkSMPL white-shark template becomes the source - and even then white-shark -> sevengill is a topology change (loss of the second dorsal, anterior->posterior migration of the single dorsal, 5->7 gill slits), which is a bigger gap than human->chimp. The paper's real value here is as the citation for 'mask-only supervision in the target domain can carry a dense surface map', which fits the lab's SAM2 mask infrastructure in SharkScarAnnotator.

Identity metric learning happens in that texture/UV space, not in image space. The repo README describes the SMALST stage as extracting "pose-invariant texture maps" and the contribution as "effective and explicit view-point normalisation" — i.e. literally the hypothesis under test in this scan.

species_domain: Grevy's zebra (Equus grevyi). Quadruped mammal.
data_requirement: CONCRETE, from the repo README: 37 individual Grevy's zebras, 4 unique images per individual, i.e. roughly 148 images total. key_numbers: 56.8% individual identification accuracy on the SMALST zebra data (37 individuals x 4 images) — VERIFIED verbatim from the repo README. The 48.0% 2D-bounding-box baseline quoted in the input record is NOT verified: the README states only the 56.8% figure and gives no comparative baseline, and I could not reach the arXiv/PDF to check. Treat "48.0% -> 56.8%, a ~9-point gain" as PLAUSIBLE BUT UNCONFIRMED. What IS confirmed is the absolute number, 56.8%, and that it comes from a 37-individual gallery.
elongate_relevance: MEDIUM-HIGH as evidence, LOW as transferable machinery. This remains the single closest END-TO-END TEST of the exact research question — map pixels onto a canonical template surface, then do re-ID in pose-free UV/texture space — and the honest headline is sobering: 56.8% on only 37 individuals with 4 images each. Read that as the realistic planning ceiling, not a floor. Three reasons a sevengill would do WORSE, not better: (1) a zebra's stripes are a far higher-contrast, higher-spatial-entropy pattern than dark-on-light sevengill speckling over a grey-brown dorsum, so there is less identity signal per UV pixel; (2) SMALST gives zebras a well-fitted, well-validated quadruped template from a mature SMAL lineage, whereas no shark has anything comparable — SharkSMPL is a single-template great-white LBS model with a 16-keypoint lamniform schema that does NOT transfer to a hexanchiform (seven gill slits not five, a single dorsal set far posterior near the pelvics so the second_dorsal_base/second_dorsal_tip keypoints have no anatomical referent, and a much longer upper caudal lobe); (3) a zebra's trunk is a near-rigid barrel between articulated limbs, so SMAL's LBS assumption holds well, whereas an anguilliform sevengill's dominant deformation is continuous lateral axial bending — precisely the mode a joint-tree LBS template approximates worst, and errors there smear the UV chart exactly across the flank where the speckle pattern lives. The methodological pipeline shape is worth copying; the accuracy expectation should be revised downward.

In Computer Vision – ECCV 2022, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer. arXiv:2207.12687. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-20086-1_21 (DOI itself unverified — Springer blocked)
license: MIT License, copyright Morphomatics — VERIFIED by fetching https://raw.githubusercontent.com/morphomatics/3Dfrom2DLandmarks/main/LICENSE. The dataset is separately citable with its own DOI 10.12752/8730; the repo asks that both paper and dataset be cited but I found no separate restrictive data license, and the repo-level MIT appears to cover the shipped .npy files. The MIT grant is a real advantage: unlike SMAL/SMPL/SMALST-derived work, nothing here is registration-gated or non-commercial.
representation_3d: Kendall shape space — a non-Euclidean (quotient-manifold) statistical shape model over SPARSE 3D landmark configurations, factoring out translation, rotation and scale. Reconstructs a 3D landmark configuration from a single monocular 2D landmark set. IMPORTANT: this is NOT DensePose/CSE and produces NO dense surface, NO UV atlas and NO per-pixel correspondence. The shipped data confirms the sparse, model-based nature: the repo's data/ directory contains only adjacency.npy (shape-model connectivity), baskingShark_basisShapes.npy (the learned PCA-analogous basis in shape space), shark.jpg and shark_2D_landmarks.npy (a single worked example) — i.e. a distributed shape BASIS, not a specimen corpus.
supervision: Manually placed 2D landmarks at inference time (not learned detection — there is no keypoint detector in this work). Training uses a corpus of 3D shapes to build the shape-space basis. Contributes a novel dataset of basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) head skeletons.
species_domain: Basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) HEAD/JAW skeletons — an elasmobranch, and specifically a LAMNIFORM, the same order as the white shark and NOT the same order as a sevengill (Hexanchiformes).
data_requirement: Views: ONE — single monocular 2D landmark set at inference; that is the paper's selling point. Landmarks: sparse, exact count NOT VERIFIED (the repo ships shark_2D_landmarks.npy but does not document its dimension in the README, and I could not open the .npy or read the paper). Training corpus size: the input record's claim of "86 basking sharks" is NOT VERIFIED and I could not corroborate it anywhere — the repo README does not state a specimen count and the data/ directory ships only the derived basis shapes, not 86 specimen files. Treat 86 as UNCONFIRMED. Resolution: not applicable (landmarks, not pixels). GPU-hours: not stated; the method is a manifold optimization, not a deep network, so compute is small — but I could not confirm a figure.
key_numbers: None verifiable. The paper's reconstruction-error tables (and the specimen count) are in the PDF, which I could not reach — arxiv.org, Springer, CVF and ECVA are all egress-blocked. Confirmed non-numeric facts: ECCV 2022, four named authors, MIT-licensed code, dataset DOI 10.12752/8730.
elongate_relevance: LOW-TO-MEDIUM, and it is important not to oversell it. Its genuine value is as the honest answer to "has anyone done 3D shape-from-images on a real shark?" — yes, exactly once, and this is it. But it models only the HEAD/jaw skeleton, so it says nothing about the elongate laterally-bending trunk that dominates the sevengill problem, and nothing about the flank surface where the speckle pattern that carries identity actually lives. It produces no dense surface and no UV space, so it cannot by itself support pose-invariant UV re-ID — it is not on the DensePose/CSE path at all. Two things it DOES offer the lab: (1) a precedent that shark-specific landmark conventions and a shark 3D shape corpus exist in the CV literature, which matters because SharkSMPL's PCA shape space is currently built from a single DigitalLife3D great-white template with 3912 verts and has no data-driven population prior; (2) an MIT-licensed, non-deep, low-data route to a shape prior. Species caveat to flag prominently: basking shark is a lamniform like the white shark, so this inherits the SAME phylogenetic mismatch as the rest of the lab's work — it does nothing to bridge to a hexanchiform with seven gill slits, a single posterior dorsal, a broad blunt head and a very long upper caudal lobe. A basking-shark head basis would not even transfer the head shape, since Cetorhinus has a hugely enlarged filter-feeding branchial basket unlike anything on a sevengill.

elongate_relevance: HIGH — the most actionable item in this chunk, and I can now make it more concrete than the input record did. Two verified escape hatches matter for Notorynchus. First, TOPOLOGY: --fg_motion=bob gives a treeless bag of bones with a freely chosen bone count, so no skeleton needs authoring at all; alternatively, authoring a NOTORYNCHUS entry in get_predefined_skeleton() is a bounded edit against a file that currently hard-codes only HUMAN (18 joints + root, no tail) and QUAD (25 joints + root, spine chain 1-4, limbs, and a 5-joint tail chain at 13-17, with QUAD_SYMM_IDX pairing limbs and leaving the tail unpaired). A sevengill skeleton is an axial chain plus paired pectorals and pelvics, a SINGLE posterior dorsal stub sitting over the pelvics (no second dorsal — the white-shark 16-keypoint Schema v2 cannot be reused), and a long asymmetric heterocercal caudal; bilateral symmetry support already exists via symm_idx and is correct for a shark. Second, and this is the bigger unlock: --feature_type=dinov2 means the CSE dependency that otherwise kills this whole family for sharks IS OPTIONAL. There is no shark or fish CSE mesh in DensePose, but DINOv2 features need no species-specific mesh — and the lab already has a DINOv2-small extractor plumbed in SharkScarAnnotator (currently ENABLED=False). Remaining honest caveat: dinov2 features give a learned canonical 3D feature field, not a 2D UV atlas, so this addresses articulation and canonicalization but is not by itself the pose-free UV space the research question asks for.

citation: Chun-Han Yao, Wei-Chih Hung, Yuanzhen Li, Michael Rubinstein, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Varun Jampani. "LASSIE: Learning Articulated Shape from Sparse Image Ensemble via 3D Part Discovery." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2022. arXiv:2207.03434

elongate_relevance: MEDIUM-HIGH, and unusually actionable for the sevengill problem — but with a real caveat the prior record understated. VERIFIED FIRST-HAND from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/lassie/main/main/skeleton.py: exactly two skeletons are hard-coded, a QUADRUPED with 17 joints, parent list [0,0,1,0,3,0,0,3,3,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12], and a BIPED with 11 joints, parent list [0,0,1,0,3,0,0,3,3,7,8]; rest joints are literal float (x,y,z) tensors uniformly scaled by 1.5 at init. Adding a sevengill skeleton — a long axial chain from snout through a posterior single dorsal to a long upper caudal lobe, plus pectoral and pelvic branches — is genuinely just a new branch with your own coordinate array and parent list, and the existing BIPED proves the pipeline is not architecturally quadruped-only. THE CAVEAT: parts are discovered/segmented via DINO feature clustering, and a sevengill is a smooth, near-convex, low-texture, limbless silhouette; the part-discovery signal that separates a zebra's four legs has very little to grab onto on an anguilliform trunk, so the axial chain may collapse. Also note the parent list has no validation — a mismatched list fails silently. Separately: this is the RIGHT family for the '16-keypoint white-shark schema does not transfer' problem, because the schema is a template you author, not a learned prior — you can drop second_dorsal_base/second_dorsal_tip, move the dorsal posterior near the pelvics, and lengthen the caudal chain without retraining anything.

citation: Chun-Han Yao, Wei-Chih Hung, Yuanzhen Li, Michael Rubinstein, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Varun Jampani. "Hi-LASSIE: High-Fidelity Articulated Shape and Skeleton Discovery from Sparse Image Ensemble." IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023. arXiv:2212.11042
license: Apache-2.0 — VERIFIED on the GitHub repo sidebar. Permissive, commercial use permitted. Repo ARCHIVED / read-only as of 2025-07-23. Google's standard 'not an officially supported Google product' disclaimer applies. Dataset licenses (Pascal-Part, LASSIE web images) are separate and not covered.
representation_3d: Class-specific 3D skeleton DISCOVERED automatically from a single user-selected reference image (no hand-authored template at all), plus shared-across-ensemble and per-instance neural part surfaces, optimized jointly with camera viewpoint and articulation. Skeleton extraction is driven by self-supervised DINO ViT features + silhouette structure.
supervision: Sparse unannotated in-the-wild image ensemble of one category. No 3D, no keypoints, no cameras, no skeleton template. One reference image must be selected by a human.
species_domain: Same nine classes as LASSIE — zebra, giraffe, tiger, elephant, kangaroo, penguin (LASSIE web images) and horse, cow, sheep (Pascal-Part). Verified from README. No aquatic, fish or elongate species.
data_requirement: VERIFIED from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/hi-lassie/main/main/config.py: rendering/optimization resolution input_size = (512, 512); DINO feature extraction at crop_size = (1024, 1024) using dino_vits8 (ViT-S/8, patch size ps=8), feature map hw=64, features PCA-reduced to d_feat=20, n_clusters=8 DINO feature clusters for part discovery, f_instance=5 deformation cutoff frequency. Environment Python 3.7 / PyTorch 1.11.0 / CUDA 11.3. README explicitly says you 'can reduce the rendering resolution by setting input_size if out of memory' — the only compute hint given. NOT STATED in the repo: images per class, GPU model, GPU-hours, batch size, number of parts. The '20-30 images per class' figure is from the paper, which I could NOT fetch (arXiv and CVF open-access both blocked this session). Views: one uncalibrated view per image; images per individual = 1 (this is a category-shape method, not an identity method).
key_numbers: Reported metrics are keypoint-transfer PCK and 2D IoU on Pascal-Part and the LASSIE image ensembles (metric names verified from the README's evaluation step). Numeric values not verifiable this session.
elongate_relevance: HIGH IN PRINCIPLE, ENTIRELY UNTESTED IN PRACTICE — this is the single most interesting cheap experiment in this chunk for the sevengill. It is the only method here that assumes NEITHER a shape template NOR a skeleton topology, which directly dissolves the stated blocker that 'the 16-keypoint white-shark schema does not transfer': Hi-LASSIE would PROPOSE its own structure for Notorynchus cepedianus rather than inherit a wrong lamniform one (no second dorsal to hallucinate, dorsal free to land posterior near the pelvics, caudal chain free to be long and asymmetric, and gill-slit count is simply not part of the representation). THE OPEN RISK, which nobody has tested: all nine demoed classes have protruding limbs, necks or wings that make DINO-cluster part discovery easy, and n_clusters is fixed at 8 in config.py. A sevengill is a smooth, near-convex, low-contrast, limbless silhouette whose only real protrusions are the fins — skeleton discovery could plausibly yield a useful axial chain with fin branches, or could degenerate into one or two blobs. Underwater turbidity and backscatter further degrade the DINO features this depends on. Verdict: cheap to try (Apache-2.0, ~20-30 images, no annotation budget), high information value either way, but do NOT plan around it succeeding. Also note the hard limitation for the actual research question: Hi-LASSIE gives an articulated canonical SHAPE, not a dense identity-preserving UV texture space — it is a step toward the canonical surface, not a re-ID system.
