species_domain: Carcharodon carcharias (white shark), aggregation sites off central California, NE Pacific population
supervision: Fully manual. Photo-identification of DORSAL FIN trailing-edge morphology only; sequential Bayesian mark-recapture with informative priors. No computer vision, no automated matching.
representation_3d: None. 2D lateral photographs of a single rigid-ish body part (the first dorsal fin). No pose normalization of any kind — the method survives by restricting itself to one fin silhouette in one stereotyped near-lateral view at the surface.
data_requirement: 3 field seasons (three-year period). 1,141 HOURS of on-water effort. Yield: 321 usable photo-IDs of 133 unique individuals — i.e. roughly 3.5 hours of effort per usable identification, and 2.4 photos per individual over three years. Yearly recapture rate 23-27%. Views: one (lateral dorsal fin at the surface). Image resolution: not stated. Camera/optics: not stated. Compute: not applicable (manual matching); GPU-hours not stated because there is no model.
key_numbers: 321 photo IDs; 133 unique individuals; 1,141 hours effort; 23-27% annual recapture; adult white shark population in central California estimated at 261 individuals, lower/upper quantile [200, 365].
license: not applicable — no code released; the abstract text itself is reproduced in SimonDedman/elasmo_analyses under GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE verified: GNU GPL Version 3, 29 June 2007)
elongate_relevance: medium — it is not a method paper and has nothing to say about UV unwrapping or lateral flexion, but it is the single most useful EFFORT/YIELD BASELINE in this chunk: 1,141 hours to get 133 individuals is the real-world denominator any sevengill re-ID pipeline must beat. Two cautions specific to your sevengill question. First, this pipeline works precisely because it uses the dorsal fin — a stiff, roughly planar, pose-stable structure — which is exactly the strategy a canonical-3D-surface approach abandons. Second, and decisively for Notorynchus: the sevengill has a SINGLE dorsal fin set far posterior near the pelvics, so the white-shark first-dorsal photo-ID protocol does not port over, and neither does the 16-keypoint Schema v2 (no second_dorsal_base / second_dorsal_tip exist on a sevengill, and the gill_slit keypoint is ambiguous across seven slits rather than five). Treat this record as the bar to clear, not as a transferable method.

representation_3d: None. 2D underwater photographs and video. No pose normalization, no template, no unwrapping.

license: not applicable — no code, no released dataset; abstract text reproduced in SimonDedman/elasmo_analyses under GPL-3.0
elongate_relevance: high — this is the strongest item in the chunk for your specific question, and it cuts AGAINST the single-channel hypothesis. Two things matter. (1) MARKING STABILITY: this is a rare direct measurement of how long natural body-surface markings persist on a carcharhinid, and the answer is 'some, 6 years' — a hedged, partial, six-year ceiling, not a lifetime-permanent signature. Your sevengill premise assumes speckled pigmentation is a durable identity channel; the closest available shark evidence says durability is partial and unquantified. (2) CHANNEL FUSION WAS MANDATORY: the authors required >=2 independent features and explicitly list fin shape AND pigmentation AND scars AND tags together. No single channel sufficed even for a human expert on a species photographed in clear Mediterranean water. That is a direct argument that a sevengill pipeline betting on scar + pigmentation in a canonical UV space should be designed as a fusion system from day one, with fin-shape and body-outline channels alongside the UV texture, and that a UV-only ablation should be treated as the expected-to-fail baseline rather than the headline. Caveat: C. plumbeus is a fusiform carcharhinid with two dorsals and five gill slits — it is closer to your white-shark schema than to Notorynchus, so it says nothing about lateral flexion or about a posterior single dorsal.

species_domain: Rhincodon typus (whale shark), Mafia Island, Tanzania, Indian Ocean, off the Rufiji River delta
supervision: Two parallel marking schemes: (a) physical numbered placard-style tags applied in situ by speargun, and (b) photo-identification via SPOT PATTERN using two unnamed software programs. Plus 8 PAT satellite tags. Semi-automated at best — the software assists a human matcher.
representation_3d: None, and the input record's caveat is correct and important. The whale-shark spot-matching standard operates on a flat, cropped 2D patch of flank immediately posterior to the fifth gill slit above the pectoral fin, taken in a near-lateral view; it applies at most an affine/planar rectification. It does NOT build or use a 3D surface, and it does NOT unwrap to a canonical UV space.
data_requirement: Two field seasons. 8 PAT-style tags deployed early 2007, durations 2-12 months. Population estimate 50-60 animals; individuals 2-8 m TL; sex ratio ~3.5:1 male-biased. NOT STATED: number of photographs, images per individual, number of views per encounter, image resolution, camera specification, matching accuracy, false-match rate, compute, GPU-hours. The abstract gives ecological results, not method performance — there is no re-ID metric in it at all.
key_numbers: Population estimate 50-60 whale sharks using the area; 8 PAT tags, 2-12 month durations; size range 2-8 m TL; sex ratio ~3.5:1 M:F; two field seasons; two unnamed spot-matching software programs.
license: not applicable — no code released with this abstract; abstract text reproduced in SimonDedman/elasmo_analyses under GPL-3.0
elongate_relevance: medium — valuable as a dated proof that automated-assisted spot-pattern re-ID was already operational in a shark by 2008, but the input record's own framing is the right one and I endorse it: the whale-shark result transfers POORLY to sevengills, and the reasons are the whole research gap. Whale sharks are photographed at 2-8 m body length, at range, in clear tropical water, in a stereotyped near-lateral glide, over a flank patch that is close to planar. Notorynchus in Californian kelp and turbid nearshore water is photographed at close range (large perspective distortion), at high and varying obliquity, and — the killer — with strong lateral body flexion, because the sevengill trunk is markedly more anguilliform and laterally flexible than a lamniform's. Under close-range strong lateral bending, a planar patch rectification breaks down in a way it never does for a whale shark, which is precisely the failure mode a canonical 3D surface + UV unwrap is meant to fix. So this abstract is best used as the MOTIVATION for the UV approach, not as evidence that flat patch matching would be sufficient. Also note this abstract reports no accuracy metric whatsoever, so it cannot serve as a performance baseline — only as an existence proof.

(1) TITLE: the input record carried a BRACKETED PLACEHOLDER — '[Region-specific anthropogenic impacts on whale sharks around the Galapagos and Eastern Pacific]' — which is a paraphrase of the first sentence of the abstract, not the title. The real title is 'Decade-long whale shark tracking from the Galapagos: identifying region specific anthropogenic risks in the Eastern Pacific'. A bracketed title is a hallucination-risk marker; it should never have shipped. Presenting author is listed as 'Sofia Green, Galapagos Whale Shark Project'; the full author line is 'Sofía M Green, Alex Hearn, Jonathan R Green, Leo Zurita, Bryan Vallejo'. SI Abstract Ref 296 and p. 23 both confirmed. (2) LICENSE WAS WRONG, AND THIS MATTERS: the record states 'Wildbook is Apache-2.0 (per WildMeOrg/Wildbook repo)'. It is NOT. I fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WildMeOrg/Wildbook/main/LICENSE and it is the GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 2, June 1991 — GPL-2.0, strong copyleft. GitHub's sidebar on github.com/WildMeOrg/Wildbook also reports GPL-2.0. The Apache-2.0 belongs to a DIFFERENT repo, WildMeOrg/wildbook-ia (the WBIA image-analysis backend), whose LICENSE.txt I fetched and confirmed as Apache License Version 2.0. And the actual modern matcher plugin, WildMeOrg/wbia-plugin-miew-id, shows NO LICENSE AT ALL on its GitHub page (only 'Copyright Conservation X Labs 2025'), which by default means all rights reserved. So the Wild Me stack is a three-license patchwork — GPL-2.0 platform / Apache-2.0 IA backend / unlicensed MiewID plugin — and you should not assume you can vendor MiewID into shark-morphometrics or SharkScarAnnotator. Flag this to whoever is making the build-vs-adopt call. (3) RETRIEVAL: the record's second claim, about a separate SI2022 abstract reporting 80 whale sharks identified via Sharkbook.ai in Malaysia, IS TRUE and I verified it — it is Li Jin Chai, Gonzalo Araujo, Nasrulhakim bin Maidin, Elvin M. Bavoh, Ruzlee Jumatin, B. Mabel Manjaji-Matsumoto, 'Malaysia Whale Sharks: distribution, seasonality and threats', SI Abstract Ref 320: 162 encounters recorded, 80 individuals identified by spot pattern, 3.5-6.0 m TL, 83% sex undetermined, with cross-border photo-ID matches Pulau Redang<->Chumphon (Thailand) and Philippines<->Pulau Sipadan (Sabah). I did NOT independently verify the record's assertion that sharkbook.ai has no Notorynchus support — www.sharkbook.ai is blocked by this session's egress proxy. Treat that as unverified. Separately: as an independent negative I grepped the ENTIRE elasmo_analyses conference corpus (167 abstract files, EEA 2002-2025, JMIH 2005-2009, SI2022) for 'Notorynchus|sevengill|seven-gill' and found only 12 hits, ALL of them telemetry, genetics, faunal-list or dentition work — plus exactly ONE genuine sevengill natural-marking ID datapoint, Jordan Housiaux (University of Otago), 'Notorynchus cepedianus in Aotearoa, New Zealand', EEA 2016 (20th Annual Conference), which reports 'photographs of unique dorsal markings (n = 23 unique individuals)' from 71 sampling trips July 2013-May 2015. That is the closest thing to sevengill photo-ID in this entire corpus and it is a manual, 23-individual conference abstract with no method and no metric. There is no automated sevengill re-ID anywhere in this corpus.
species_domain: Rhincodon typus (whale shark), Galapagos Marine Reserve and the Eastern Tropical Pacific
supervision: Spot-pattern photo-identification submitted to and matched through the global sharkbook.ai catalogue (Wildbook for Sharks), combined with satellite telemetry. Matching is semi-automated: an algorithm proposes candidates, a human confirms. Connectivity/population indices derived by lagged-identification-rate models over the Galapagos photo-ID dataset; spatial analysis in QGIS and R.
representation_3d: None. 2D spot-pattern matching on a flank patch. Wildbook's classical shark matcher is a planar spot-constellation method; the newer MiewID path is a 2D deep embedding. Neither builds a 3D surface and neither unwraps to canonical UV.
data_requirement: Decade of effort: 2011-2021. 106 whale sharks tagged with 129 satellite tags, 124 of which yielded analysable data. 522 individuals identified through sharkbook.ai over that period. NOT STATED anywhere in the abstract: photographs per individual, number of views per encounter, image resolution, matching precision/recall, false-match rate, training set size, compute or GPU-hours. This is an ecology abstract; it reports catalogue size, not model performance. If you need per-individual image counts for a sharkbook-style catalogue you will have to get them from the Wild Me / MiewID papers, not from here.
key_numbers: 2011-2021; 106 whale sharks tagged, 129 tags, 124 analysable; 522 individuals identified via the sharkbook.ai global catalogue. (Companion SI2022 abstract, Ref 320: 162 Malaysian encounters, 80 individuals spot-pattern identified 1996-2021, two international photo-ID matches.)
code_url: https://github.com/WildMeOrg/Wildbook (platform); https://github.com/WildMeOrg/wildbook-ia (image-analysis backend); https://github.com/WildMeOrg/wbia-plugin-miew-id (MiewID matcher plugin). Catalogue front end at sharkbook.ai — data itself is not open.
license: SPLIT AND PARTLY UNLICENSED — do not treat as one license. WildMeOrg/Wildbook = GPL-2.0 (verified: raw LICENSE on both main and master is 'GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 2, June 1991'; GitHub sidebar agrees). WildMeOrg/wildbook-ia = Apache-2.0 (verified: LICENSE.txt = 'Apache License Version 2.0, January 2004'). WildMeOrg/wbia-plugin-miew-id = NO LICENSE FILE OR SIDEBAR LICENSE FOUND, only 'Copyright Conservation X Labs 2025' — i.e. all-rights-reserved by default. sharkbook.ai catalogue data: not open. The input record's blanket 'Wildbook is Apache-2.0' is incorrect.
elongate_relevance: medium for the science, high for the engineering decision. Scientifically this is another whale-shark planar-flank result and inherits every one of the transfer problems listed under the Potenski record — stereotyped lateral pose, near-planar patch, clear water, large scale — none of which hold for a laterally-flexing Notorynchus in Californian nearshore water. It contributes no pose-normalization method and no 3D anything. Its real value to you is threefold. (1) It fixes the ORDER OF MAGNITUDE at which pattern-based shark re-ID is proven to operate: 522 individuals over a decade, basin-scale, with confirmed cross-border matches — that is the demonstrated ceiling for 2D spot matching in a shark, and it is a genuinely high bar. (2) It identifies the incumbent production system you would be competing with or plugging into, which is directly relevant to SharkScarAnnotator's currently-manual shark_catalog: adopting Wildbook/MiewID is a live alternative to building your own matcher, and consistent with your own prior pass's recommendation of MiewID-msv3 over raw DINOv2. (3) The license split above is the blocker on that path — GPL-2.0 on the platform is viral for anything you link into it, and the MiewID plugin has no license at all, so 'just use MiewID' is not yet a clean option and needs a direct ask to Wild Me / Conservation X Labs before you build on it. Nothing here addresses the seven-gill-slit / single-posterior-dorsal keypoint schema problem; that remains unsolved in the literature I could reach.

elongate_relevance: medium, and the reason is the argument rather than the animal. A flat rajid batoid is morphologically irrelevant to a hexanchiform. This is direct empirical support for the lab's own prior conclusion that scars are an unproven re-ID signature, and it applies with extra force to sevengills, whose claimed identity signal is scar + pigmentation: the pigmentation half may be stable, the scar half demonstrably is not in at least two elasmobranchs.

citation: Natalia Neverova, Artsiom Sanakoyeu, David Novotny, Patrick Labatut, Andrea Vedaldi. "Discovering Relationships between Object Categories via Universal Canonical Maps." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2021. arXiv:2106.09758 (arXiv ID NOT verified - arxiv.org is blocked in this environment; cite the CVPR proceedings form).
correction_note: CITATION CONFIRMED VERBATIM. I fetched the official detectron2 DensePose CSE doc and its BibTeX block reads exactly: @InProceedings{Neverova2021UniversalCanonicalMaps, title={Discovering Relationships between Object Categories via Universal Canonical Maps}, author={Neverova, Natalia and Sanakoyeu, Artsiom and Novotny, David and Labatut, Patrick and Vedaldi, Andrea}, journal={The IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)}, year={2021}}. (The official BibTeX misuses 'journal' for a conference; the canonical form is CVPR proceedings.) TWO CORRECTIONS to the record: (1) 'The same 13 tetrapod meshes' is right on the count but needs unpacking - I fetched projects/DensePose/densepose/data/meshes/builtin.py and it registers exactly 13 meshes: smpl_27554, chimp_5029, cat_5001, cat_7466, sheep_5004, zebra_5002, horse_5004, giraffe_5002, elephant_5002, dog_5002, dog_7466, cow_5002, bear_4936. That is 1 human + 12 animal meshes but only 10 distinct categories (cat and dog each appear at two resolutions), and the CSE annotation set covers only 9 animal categories (bear, cow, cat, dog, elephant, giraffe, horse, sheep, zebra). All placental mammals; zero non-tetrapods, zero fish, zero elongate bodies. (2) The record's claim that the m2m/i2m 16k checkpoints are the UCM cycle-loss outputs is CORRECT and I verified it: DENSEPOSE_CSE.md states the ds2 animal models are trained 'with soft assignment loss and, for some schedules, cycle losses' and points to 'Neverova et al, 2021' for the cycle losses (the link href is literally empty in the doc). I could NOT fetch the CVPR paper itself, so all paper-internal claims (method details beyond cycle losses, the full experimental protocol) remain unverified from primary text.
representation_3d: Per-category 3D template meshes (13 registered) tied together by mesh-to-mesh (m2m) and image-to-mesh (i2m) cycle-consistency losses on top of Continuous Surface Embeddings; each mesh vertex gets a learned embedding, and pixels are matched to vertices by embedding similarity. Not a flat UV atlas - a vertex-embedding space.
supervision: Cross-category cycle consistency on top of extremely sparse manual CSE point correspondences (~3 annotated points per instance) plus instance segmentation masks. No dense per-pixel ground truth for animals.
species_domain: 9 annotated animal categories (bear, cow, cat, dog, elephant, giraffe, horse, sheep, zebra) + human, over 13 registered meshes.
code_url: https://github.com/facebookresearch/detectron2 (projects/DensePose; cse configs densepose_rcnn_R_50_FPN_soft_animals_I0_finetune_m2m_16k.yaml and _i2m_16k.yaml). No standalone UCM repo exists - the method ships only as detectron2 configs/checkpoints.

CAUTION, NOT VERIFIED: the pretrained meshes/checkpoints are served from dl.fbaipublicfiles.com and I found no separate license file for them in-repo; the smpl_27554 mesh is SMPL-topology-derived, and SMPL itself is under an MPI non-commercial EULA. I could not confirm or refute whether that flows through - check before any commercial use.
data_requirement: VERIFIED from projects/DensePose/doc/DENSEPOSE_DATASETS.md. Cycle-loss models train on DensePose-LVIS ds2_train: 1203 categories / 99,388 images / 1,270,141 segmentation annotations overall, of which the animal CSE subset is 13,746 images, 46,964 segmentation annotations and 18,932 DensePose annotations at ~3 annotated points per instance (i.e. only ~57k point correspondences total across 9 species). Predecessor ds1_train: 556 cat / 4,141 images / 23,985 segm; animal subset 4,141 images / 9,472 segm / 5,184 dp. Compute (VERIFIED from the CSE model zoo table): 16k-iteration schedule, 0.386 s/iter and 8.4 GB train memory for the no-cycle baseline, 0.508 s/iter and 12.2 GB for m2m, 0.483 s/iter and 9.7 GB for i2m; inference ~0.056-0.058 s/image. Total GPU-hours not stated. Images per individual: N/A - this is category-level correspondence, not individual ID.
key_numbers: VERIFIED from the DENSEPOSE_CSE.md ds2 animal model zoo. Baseline R_50_FPN_soft_animals_I0_finetune_16k (no cycle loss): box AP 54.2, segm AP 67.0, dp.AP_GPS 29.0, dp.AP_GPSm 38.6, GErr 13.2, GPS 85.4. With mesh-to-mesh cycle loss (m2m_16k): 54.1 / 67.3 / 28.6 / 38.4 / GErr 12.5 / GPS 87.6. With image-to-mesh cycle loss (i2m_16k): 54.0 / 66.6 / 28.9 / 38.3 / GErr 11.0 / GPS 88.9. READ THIS CAREFULLY: the cycle losses cut geodesic error 13.2 -> 11.0 (~17% relative) and raise GPS 85.4 -> 88.9, but detection/segmentation AP and dp.AP_GPS are FLAT or slightly WORSE. The benefit is correspondence smoothness, not detection accuracy, and it costs ~25-30% more training time and up to 45% more GPU memory.
elongate_relevance: low - NEGATIVE, and the verified mesh inventory hardens the record's judgment. Every one of the 13 meshes is a quadruped tetrapod or a human; cycle consistency is learned between surfaces that share a limbed, five-part topology (head, torso, four limbs, tail). A sevengill has no limbs to put in correspondence, an anguilliform trunk with continuous lateral bending, seven gill slits, and a single posterior dorsal - there is no source category in this set to bootstrap from, and the ~3-points-per-instance supervision regime assumes an annotator can name a semantically stable landmark, which on a featureless elongate flank is exactly what is missing. Its one genuinely transferable lesson is negative-cost information: FAIR needed ~19k sparsely-annotated instances across 9 species to get GErr 11, so a single-species sevengill CSE from scratch is not a small annotation job.

THE MATERIAL CORRECTION IS THE LICENSE. The record says 'MIT (verified by fetching LICENSE.txt)' - that is true but INCOMPLETE AND DECISION-MISLEADING. The repo ships TWO license files. LICENSE.txt is indeed plain MIT (copyright 'silviazuffi', 2018, no non-commercial clause) and covers the CODE. But LICENSE_SMAL_MODEL.txt is the Max Planck 'Software Copyright License for non-commercial scientific research purposes', which covers the SMAL Data & Software including 3D meshes, images, videos, textures, scripts and animations, and states verbatim: 'Any other use, in particular any use for commercial purposes, is prohibited... This license also prohibits the use of the Data & Software to train methods/algorithms/neural networks/etc for commercial use of any kind.' It also forbids redistribution and requires emailing ps-license@tue.mpg.de for commercial licensing. SEPARATELY, README.md instructs 'download the SMPL model' from ps.is.tuebingen.mpg.de/code/smpl - a registration + non-commercial EULA gate. NET: the MIT badge in the sidebar is on the code only; the animal shape model this whole method depends on is research/non-commercial with an explicit no-commercial-training clause. Also correcting a practical point the record omits: the code is Python 2.7 / PyTorch 0.5.0 and depends on Neural Mesh Renderer - this stack is severely bit-rotted and is a port, not a run. FINALLY, the record's WildlifeDatasets claim is now VERIFIED EXACTLY, not merely reported: wildlife_datasets/datasets/smalst.py records reported_n_individuals=10, real_animals=False, reported_n_total=12850, size=11978, span='artificial', wild=False, licenses='MIT License'.

Predicted UV texture map 256x256 (nnutils/smal_mesh_net.py: texture_img_size=256, tex_size=6 per face). Training run in scripts/smalst_train_run.sh: --num_images=20000 (cap on synthetic training renders), --num_epochs=200, --save_epoch_freq=20, --batch_size=2, --do_validation=True; an earlier commented variant uses 40 epochs with nz_feat=16. Per-image test-time optimization (scripts/smalst_op_run.sh) runs a further 220 epochs at batch_size=1, lr=1e-4, PER IMAGE - budget for that. Dataloader default num_images=3000, n_data_workers=4. ACTUAL RELEASED DATASET SIZE: 11,978 images / 12,850 reported, over 10 synthetic individuals (~1,200 images per individual) - VERIFIED from wildlife-datasets smalst.py. Views per individual: 'multiple', exact count not stated. GPU-hours: NOT STATED anywhere in the repo.
key_numbers: The repo reports no headline metric table; the paper (unreachable here) is where pose/shape/texture numbers live, so I am not quoting any. What I CAN state as verified: 10 individuals, 11,978 released images, 256x256 in and 256x256 UV out, 3,889-vertex template, 28 keypoints, 200 epochs at batch 2 over up to 20,000 renders. NO re-ID accuracy number exists in the release, and the record's caveat (a) is confirmed by absence.
elongate_relevance: medium-high as a METHOD PRECEDENT, low as EVIDENCE. This is the closest published thing to 'regress an individual's pigmentation pattern as a UV texture on a canonical animal template', and it does so from an almost entirely synthetic training set at a template complexity nearly identical to the asker's shark mesh (3,889 vs 3,912 verts) - which directly de-risks the Blender-render + SharkSMPL strategy for a speckled sevengill. But the honest reading is harsher than the record's: with real_animals=False and reported_n_individuals=10, SMALST has NEVER been shown to re-identify a real animal. It demonstrates that texture-on-template is LEARNABLE, not that UV-space matching BEATS 2D matching. Structurally it is also a quadruped SMAL model - the kinematic tree, the shape space and the 28-keypoint schema are all limbed-mammal, so nothing transfers to an anguilliform trunk except the pipeline shape. And the non-commercial SMAL/SMPL encumbrance means the asker cannot legally reuse the actual model assets in anything commercial, only re-implement the idea on their own DigitalLife3D template.

citation: Zhedong Zheng, Xiaohan Wang, Nenggan Zheng, Yi Yang. "Parameter-Efficient Person Re-identification in the 3D Space." IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems (TNNLS), 2022. DOI: 10.1109/TNNLS.2022.3214834. arXiv:2006.04569.
correction_note: AUTHOR LIST WAS WRONG. The input record omitted Xiaohan Wang. The authors' own BibTeX in the official repo README reads: Zheng, Zhedong and Wang, Xiaohan and Zheng, Nenggan and Yang, Yi. Also adds DOI 10.1109/TNNLS.2022.3214834, which the record lacked. Everything else in the record checked out: TNNLS 2022, arXiv:2006.04569, MIT license, and the 'last push July 2026' claim (most recent commit on master is 2026-07-06, 'Update README.md' 5a0bda9 — but note that is a README touch, the substantive code is from 2022). representation_3d: Per-image reconstructed 3D point cloud with per-point RGB. CONFIRMED from README: the 3D data is generated by a fork of HMR (https://github.com/layumi/hmr) and the authors explicitly 'remove all 3D faces and only keep 3D points positions & RGB to save the storage & loading burden.' supervision: Standard re-ID identity labels only (plus circle-loss variants). The 3D lift is a frozen off-the-shelf HMR pass done as preprocessing, not learned jointly. key_numbers: From the repo README results table (Rank-1 / mAP): Market-1501 OG-Net 86.82/69.02, OG-Net-Small 86.79/67.92, OG-Net+Circle 87.80/70.56, OG-Net-Deep+Circle 88.81/72.91. MSMT17: OG-Net 44.27/21.57, OG-Net+Circle 45.28/22.81, OG-Net-Deep+Circle 47.32/24.07. CONTEXT THE RECORD IS RIGHT ABOUT: these are NOT state-of-the-art numbers for 2022 2D re-ID (strong 2D baselines were >95 Rank-1 on Market-1501 by then). The paper's selling point is parameter efficiency, not accuracy.
data_requirement: GPU memory >= 4 GB (README cites a single GTX 1080 as sufficient) — this is an unusually cheap method to reproduce. Input is single-view, single-image per sample; no multi-view requirement. Pretrained snapshots for all four datasets are shipped in ./snapshot. NOT STATED in the repo: exact parameter counts, input image resolution, number of points per cloud, training wall-clock/GPU-hours. I could not retrieve those from the paper because arXiv is blocked — do not quote a parameter count for this paper without checking the PDF.

If you only consume the precomputed point clouds this does not bite you; if you run the lift yourself it does.
elongate_relevance: MEDIUM. Useful as a conceptual counter-example rather than a transferable method: it shows canonicalization does not have to mean a UV atlas — you can just encode XYZ+RGB directly. But three things blunt it for sevengills. (1) It is NOT pose-invariant in the sense the research question asks: the point cloud is reconstructed per-image and still carries the subject's pose, so a laterally-bending sevengill body produces a differently-shaped cloud each frame; the graph network is asked to be tolerant of that, not to remove it. A canonical-surface UV map genuinely removes it. (2) The lift is HMR, i.e. hard-wired to SMPL humans. For a sevengill you would need the asker's SharkSMPL lift, which is a white-shark template — wrong gill count, wrong dorsal topology (single posterior dorsal, no second dorsal), and far too stiff a trunk for an anguilliform hexanchiform. (3) Identity here comes from clothing colour over a coarse cloud; sevengill identity is a fine speckle pattern, and dropping faces/texture to bare coloured points is exactly the wrong compression for high-frequency pigmentation. Worth citing in a related-work section; not worth building on.

elongate_relevance: HIGH — and the record's framing is right, so I am reinforcing rather than revising it. This is the strongest cost argument against building a canonical-surface UV pipeline for sevengills. Vehicles are the easiest possible case for surface-aligned re-ID: perfectly rigid, an exact CAD model exists, unlimited labelled synthetic data, no deformation at all. PAMTRI had every reason to map to a canonical surface and did not — it fused pose as heatmap/segment input channels and won ICCV. If surface mapping does not pay for itself on rigid cars, the prior that it pays on a laterally-bending hexanchiform is weak. Second, the architectural match to the asker's existing stack is near-exact: PAMTRI's keypoint-heatmap-plus-segment channel stack IS the shark-morphometrics 19-channel proxy input (16 keypoint heatmaps + 2 flow + 1 edge), and PAMTRI's 'highly randomized synthetic data' IS the domain-randomized Blender pipeline in shark-pose-3d. The asker has already built PAMTRI for sharks without calling it that. Third, and important for the species problem: a heatmap-channel approach degrades gracefully under schema change. Dropping second_dorsal_base/second_dorsal_tip and re-siting the dorsal posteriorly is a channel-count edit and a retrain; it does not require re-authoring a template mesh, a skinning weight map, or a UV atlas. The seven-gill-slit issue is likewise just a relabeling of one keypoint (or an expansion to a gill-slit series) rather than a topology change. That asymmetry in migration cost is the single most decision-relevant fact in this chunk.

elongate_relevance: HIGH — I agree with the record that this is the most important comparison in the scan, and the verification makes the argument sharper. This is the same lab, same species, same data, evaluated first WITHOUT a canonical surface (local affine-covariant patches) and later WITH UV unwrapping. That controlled pair is the only honest measurement anywhere of what canonical-surface normalization actually buys for pattern-based animal re-ID, made by the people most motivated for it to look large. CAVEAT I MUST ADD: the size of that delta ('up to 5.4%') is NOT verified in this chunk — it must be confirmed against arXiv 2506.15369 before it anchors any decision. For sevengills specifically, NORPPA is close to an ideal template: a segmented flank bearing a high-frequency speckled pattern, matched by affine-invariant local features, with retrieval-style enrollment that needs no retraining per new individual — which is exactly what SharkScarAnnotator's manual shark_catalog needs to become automated. And it is species-schema-free: no keypoints, no kinematic tree, no template mesh, so the seven-gill-slit / single-posterior-dorsal problem simply never arises. The one genuine mismatch is that HesAffNet's local affine model assumes patches are locally planar and only affinely warped; a strongly laterally-bending anguilliform trunk produces larger out-of-plane curvature across the flank than a hauled-out seal does, so the affine assumption is under more strain here than in the seal case. That is precisely the gap a UV unwrap would close — which is why the NORPPA-vs-unwrapping delta is the number that decides this project.

elongate_relevance: HIGH, and it is the right first experiment. Local-feature correspondence with LightGlue/LoFTR is pose-tolerant with no canonical space at all — the correspondence field absorbs the lateral bend directly, and unlike NORPPA's HesAffNet the learned matchers are not restricted to a local affine warp, so they should tolerate a strongly flexing anguilliform trunk better. It sidesteps every species-schema problem for free: no keypoints, no kinematic tree, no template mesh, so seven gill slits, a single posterior dorsal, and the missing second dorsal are all simply non-issues — nothing in the pipeline knows what a dorsal fin is. Enrollment is retrieval-style, which is what SharkScarAnnotator's manual shark_catalog actually needs. This is also the asker's own prior recommendation, now confirmed real, released, actively documented and MIT at the code layer. TWO HONEST CAVEATS. First, the fusion is expensive at query time — it is 6 matchers per pair, which is why the docs push the 100-pair shortlist budget; over 4850 video files that matters and needs measuring, not assuming. Second, the weights question above: MIT code plus probably-non-commercial weights is a real constraint if this ever leaves the lab. The honest research plan is: run WildFusion (or even just LightGlue+ALIKED alone) on segmented sevengill flanks first, get a number in days, and only then decide whether a canonical-surface UV pipeline — which is a multi-quarter effort requiring a sevengill template mesh that does not exist — is worth attempting to beat it.

elongate_relevance: HIGH — and it is the single strongest NEGATIVE data point against the UV-unwrap plan. This is the closest species analogue that exists (large elongate laterally-flexible speckle-patterned elasmobranch, shot underwater from arbitrary angles), the field has run individual ID on it for 30 years, and the verified implementation shows the normalization is THREE MANUALLY PLACED REFERENCE SPOTS PER FLANK feeding a triangle-similarity matcher — no template, no mesh, no UV. Two further transfers to sevengills: (1) left and right are maintained as ENTIRELY SEPARATE spot sets, so bilateral pigmentation is treated as asymmetric and non-mirrorable — the same assumption must hold for a sevengill speckle chart, which kills any single shared UV atlas and doubles the enrollment burden; (2) the reference-spot trick is a cheap, robust substitute for the asker's 16-keypoint schema and is species-agnostic — it needs no second dorsal fin and no five-gill assumption, so unlike the white-shark Schema v2 it transfers to Notorynchus cepedianus unchanged. Recommend Arzoumanian-2005-style constellation matching on the sevengill speckle field as baseline zero, with Bonner & Holmberg 2013 as the mark-recapture statistics for imperfect marks.

elongate_relevance: MEDIUM. The species is wrong in almost every way that matters (rigid terrestrial trunk, no lateral undulation, high-contrast binary stripes rather than low-contrast speckles, above-water lighting) so it is not a performance predictor. Its value is purely as METHODOLOGICAL PRIOR ART for the cheapest rung on the ladder: 'pose normalization' here means a 2D flank rectification, and that was sufficient to sustain a decade of real field biometrics. For sevengills the direct analogue is to rectify the flank crop along the body axis. But note the specific failure mode the asker inherits: a zebra flank is nearly planar and nearly rigid, so a rectangular rectification is close to correct; a sevengill's anguilliform trunk bends laterally within a single frame, so a rigid rectangle is NOT the right rectification. The correct cheap analogue is a CURVED-AXIS (spine-following) unroll — fit a centreline through the asker's existing keypoints and resample perpendicular to it — not the rectangle StripeSpotter used. Also, the 45-individual / 820-image scale is a useful floor: a working flank-pattern biometric was demonstrated at that size, so a sevengill pilot does not need thousands of individuals to be publishable.

key_numbers: 24,578 images; 9,861 individuals; ~2.5 images/individual; 7-year span (2018-2024); 27.7 GB; 16 head/body keypoints + 4 calibration-card keypoints; 3 bbox parts (body/head/headless); left+right sides labelled. No re-ID accuracy figure recoverable (publisher blocked). Largest fish individual-ID dataset located in this scan.
elongate_relevance: HIGH for schema design, LOW as a pose-normalization method. Four transfers, in order of value: (1) IT IS AN EXISTING 16-POINT FISH KEYPOINT SCHEMA and it is organized around OPERCULAR (gill-cover) landmarks — bottom_opercular, top_opercular, medium_opercular, eyes_opercular — rather than around a two-dorsal-fin lamniform body plan. That is exactly the axis on which the asker's white-shark Schema v2 breaks for Notorynchus cepedianus (seven gill slits, single posterior dorsal, no second dorsal). Melops is a published precedent for redesigning the schema around the head/gill region and the fins the animal actually has, at the same cardinality of 16, so the asker's tooling and YOLOv8n-pose head need no architectural change — only a relabel. (2) THE WHITE COLOUR-CALIBRATION CARD plus colour_extraction_correction.csv is the single most transferable engineering idea here: if sevengill identity rests on dark-on-light SPECKLE pigmentation, then colour and exposure normalization is load-bearing, and underwater imagery is far worse for it than a Norwegian sampling board. The asker has none of this in the 661 GB archive. (3) ASYMMETRY: the identity pattern is explicitly asymmetric left vs right, with 'side' tracked as a first-class column — the same conclusion the Wildbook source reaches independently for whale sharks. Two independent species precedents now say a single shared UV chart across the midline is wrong, and that mirror augmentation will corrupt identity. (4) THE NEGATIVE RESULT: at 9,861 individuals and ~2.5 images each, the fish-ID field's answer to pose variance is to CONSTRAIN CAPTURE (hand-held, standardized lateral, calibration card) rather than to normalize computationally. That is a data-side substitute for the whole UV pipeline, and the asker — with 661 GB of video across 4 sites and 14 years — can be brutally selective about near-lateral frames at essentially zero method cost. Caveat on transfer: a captured, hand-held, board-mounted wrasse is nearly rigid and nearly planar; a free-swimming sevengill is neither, so the capture-constraint strategy degrades, and this dataset gives no evidence about how far.

key_numbers: 37,440 real camera-trap images; 219 individuals; ~171 images/individual; 15-year span; 20-point skeletons; instance masks; >100,000 synthetic Unity + diffusion-texture images; 3 evaluation protocols (geo-aware, time-aware open-set, time-aware closed-set); 2 regions. Published Scientific Data, February 2026.
elongate_relevance: HIGH as an EXPERIMENT-DESIGN TEMPLATE, LOW as a method — and the input record's framing of it that way is correct and worth keeping. Four specific transfers: (1) THE 20-POINT SKELETON IS THE PRECEDENT THE ASKER NEEDS TO CITE. The authors did not force the 17-point COCO-animal schema onto a lynx; they designed a species-appropriate 20-point skeleton. That is the published justification for abandoning the white-shark 16-keypoint Schema v2 for Notorynchus cepedianus rather than trying to force-fit it — no second_dorsal_base/second_dorsal_tip exist, first_dorsal sits far posterior near the pelvics, and gill_slit is one of seven not five. Pair this with Melops's opercular-centred 16-point fish schema as the second precedent. (2) THE TIME-AWARE OPEN-SET PROTOCOL IS EXACTLY THE EVALUATION A SCAR-BASED CLAIM REQUIRES. Scars accumulate and heal; pigmentation may drift with growth. A random split will massively overstate performance. Adopt split-time_open as the headline protocol and report the closed-set number only as a ceiling. This is the highest-value thing in the record. (3) THE UNITY + DIFFUSION-TEXTURE SYNTHETIC PIPELINE IS A DIRECT MODEL FOR THE ASKER'S EXISTING BLENDER SETUP. shark-pose-3d already domain-randomizes synthetic Blender renders for pose; CzechLynx shows how to extend the same rig to generate IDENTITY-LABELLED synthetic individuals by varying the coat/skin texture — which is the only tractable way to get thousands of labelled sevengill identities, since real speckle-pattern ground truth is scarce. 100k synthetic to 37k real is the ratio they found worth building. (4) LIMITS: a lynx is a rigid quadruped photographed by a fixed camera trap in air; nothing about its pose statistics, its lateral flexibility, or its imaging conditions predicts a free-swimming anguilliform shark underwater, and the paper contributes NOTHING on canonical 3D surface mapping. Cite it for protocol and schema, never for method.

elongate_relevance: MEDIUM - and lower than the input record claims. Split the value in two. (a) BACKBONE EVIDENCE: if the +0.13-vs-+0.03 result holds, it independently corroborates the lab's own prior conclusion that raw DINOv2 is the wrong backbone and domain-specific MiewID/MegaDescriptor-class models are right - which bears on the hard-disabled DINOv2-small 384-d track signature extractor in SharkScarAnnotator and the untrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 in shark-scar-classifier. But that entire argument rests on numbers I could NOT verify, so it is currently a lead, not evidence. (b) OPEN-SET FRAMING: the BAKS/BAUS-style known/unknown split is the correct evaluation shape for a growing sevengill catalog where most encounters are new animals - genuinely useful, and it is a real gap in SharkScarAnnotator's manual shark_catalog, which has no automated matching and no open-set notion at all. (c) RELEVANCE TO THE ACTUAL RESEARCH QUESTION: LOW. This paper has no 3D representation, no template, no UV space, and no pose normalization of any kind. It cannot tell you whether canonical 3D surface mapping works for sevengills; it is a 2D-embedding baseline you would benchmark such a method AGAINST. (d) SEVENGILL-SPECIFIC: nothing here is elongate-body-aware. elongate_relevance: MEDIUM - genuinely useful mechanism, but the input record overstates it on three counts. WHY IT MATTERS: feature-space normalization is the one approach in this chunk that requires NO canonical template, NO UV atlas, and NO keypoint-schema redesign. That directly sidesteps the hardest sevengill blocker: SharkSMPL's single template mesh is a DigitalLife3D great white (3912 verts, five gill slits, two dorsals, lamniform caudal), and the 16-keypoint Schema v2 does not transfer to a hexanchiform - second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip have no anatomical referent on Notorynchus cepedianus, first_dorsal sits far posterior near the pelvics rather than mid-trunk, and 'gill_slit' is ambiguous across seven slits rather than five. A curvature-conditioned feature transform needs only a bend estimate, and the existing body_midpoint_dorsal / body_midpoint_ventral / caudal_notch chain plus a re-based sevengill keypoint set could supply that far more cheaply than building SharkSMPL-for-sevengills. THREE CAVEATS THE RECORD OMITS. (1) The measured pose-invariance gain is +0.25 pp on the cross-pose benchmark - a marginal win, not a step change, and not obviously worth a new module. (2) Face pose is a 3-DOF RIGID rotation of a near-rigid object; sevengill pose is a high-DOF NON-RIGID spinal bend of an anguilliform trunk, plus independent fin articulation. The paper offers zero evidence the feature transform generalizes from rigid rotation to non-rigid deformation, and the conditioning variable is qualitatively harder. (3) The method is built on 5.1M images / 93k identities of pretraining plus 532k pose-simulated pairs. A sevengill catalog will not have that. The transferable idea, however, is cheap to test: the existing Blender pipeline can synthesize the sevengill analogue of MS1M-Pose-Sim (same synthetic individual rendered across a bend sweep), which is exactly the paired supervision this method needs and exactly what the lab already knows how to produce.

elongate_relevance: HIGH on mechanism - the strongest of the four for the actual research question - but with a real deformation-gap caveat. WHY HIGH: (1) TOPOLOGY FITS. DensePose's answer to dense correspondence is a 24-chart body atlas with seam handling designed for a limbed biped. A shark has no limbs and unwraps naturally to a SINGLE continuous strip, so one UV position map suffices with no chart-boundary design at all - which is precisely the kind of simplification PRNet's single-image formulation gives you. (2) THE TRAINING TARGETS ARE FREE. PRNet needed 3DMM fits over 300W-LP to make its targets; this lab can render UV position maps directly out of Blender as a perfect-ground-truth pass, the same trick, at zero annotation cost, reusing the existing domain-randomized synthetic pipeline from shark-pose-3d. (3) IT IS DRASTICALLY SIMPLER than the current stack - one feed-forward encoder-decoder replaces ResNet-50 + IEF/SPIN + Neural Descent (HUND) + BiLSTM + Skeletor, and runs at >100 fps, which matters for a 661 GB archive. (4) IT PRODUCES EXACTLY THE OBJECT THE RESEARCH QUESTION ASKS FOR: a per-pixel map to a fixed canonical surface coordinate, in which speckle/spot pigmentation and scar positions can be compared pose-free. SEVENGILL-SPECIFIC CAVEATS. (a) PRNet does not remove the need for a template - it relocates it to target generation. You still must author a Notorynchus cepedianus template with its own UV layout, and SharkSMPL's great-white mesh will not serve: seven gill slits not five, a SINGLE dorsal set far posterior near the pelvics with no second dorsal, a strongly heterocercal elongate caudal with a very long upper lobe, a broad blunt head, and a markedly more anguilliform trunk. The 16-keypoint Schema v2 must be revised before any of this: second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip must be dropped, first_dorsal_base/tip re-anchored posteriorly, and gill_slit disambiguated across seven slits. (b) DEFORMATION GAP. PRNet was validated on faces, which are near-rigid and vary mostly by 3-DOF viewpoint plus mild expression. A sevengill's identity-bearing flank is on a laterally-bending, high-DOF trunk. Nothing in PRNet's evidence base speaks to regressing a position map through large non-rigid bending, and that is the single biggest technical risk in porting it. (c) The pigmentation signal is the right target for this representation - dark-on-light speckling over a grey-brown dorsum is a dense, spatially-distributed pattern, which is exactly what UV-space comparison is good at, and notably better suited to it than sparse scars, which the lab's own prior pass already concluded are an unproven re-ID signature.

elongate_relevance: high — and this is the strongest theoretical argument in the whole chunk that a bending shark trunk is an EASY case rather than a hard one. Functional maps assume near-isometric deformation, and lateral undulation of an elongate body is near-isometric: anguilliform bending changes extrinsic shape while preserving the intrinsic surface metric, so the Laplace-Beltrami spectrum, and hence the spectral basis the correspondence is expressed in, is nearly invariant to how the sevengill is flexed in any given frame. That is precisely the pose-invariance the research question is asking for, obtained by construction rather than by learning. Four caveats, all real: (1) fins flex non-isometrically and the sevengill's single far-posterior dorsal plus its very long upper caudal lobe are exactly the high-curvature extremities where spectral methods degrade; (2) seven gill slits opening and closing, and jaw protrusion, are local non-isometries near the head — and the seven-slit head is also the region where the white-shark template is most wrong; (3) an elongate body is close to symmetric about its long axis, and intrinsic symmetry is the classic, well-documented failure mode of spectral matching — a sevengill risks head-tail or left-right flips that a compact quadruped does not; (4) nothing in FAUST/SCAPE/SMAL/DT4D tests an anguilliform body, so the near-isometry argument is sound in theory but UNTESTED on this body plan. Also flag the schema mismatch upstream: this method needs meshes, not keypoints, and the 16-keypoint white-shark Schema v2 does not transfer (no second dorsal on a sevengill, so second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip are undefined; first_dorsal_base/tip sit near the pelvics rather than mid-body; gill_slit is one landmark for a five-slit animal being applied to a seven-slit one).

elongate_relevance: medium — enabling infrastructure rather than a result, but with one genuine elongate-specific gotcha. Favourable: discretization-agnosticism means a shark template remeshed from the DigitalLife3D geometry (or from a future sevengill scan, which is what would actually be needed) is fine, and heat diffusion is an INTRINSIC operator, so it inherits the same near-isometry-under-lateral-bending advantage argued for ULRSSM. The gotcha the record correctly identifies: diffusion time is a learned but globally-scaled parameter, and on a body roughly 3x more elongate than the quadrupeds and humans it was tuned on, the learned time-scales may land wrong — a diffusion radius that is informative on a compact SMAL quadruped can be simultaneously too local to span a sevengill's trunk and too global to resolve individual speckles. Expect to retune diffusion-time initialisation/range rather than accept defaults. Second point: the features are intrinsic, so they describe geometry, not pigmentation; on a sevengill the identity signal is the dark-on-light speckle pattern, which is a TEXTURE signal this backbone does not see. DiffusionNet gets you the correspondence; the speckle comparison has to happen afterwards in the UV/texture domain.

elongate_relevance: high — this is the entry that matches the lab's actual operating condition, and the candidate record's reasoning is sound and worth keeping. Every real sevengill sighting in a 661GB video archive is a PARTIAL observation: one flank only, cropped by the frame edge, degraded by turbidity, occluded by kelp, often mid-swim. Full-to-full correspondence methods such as ULRSSM silently assume the whole animal is visible, which is close to never true here; DPFM is the specific formulation for mapping a partial surface onto a complete canonical template. The elongate-specific amplification: partiality is strictly WORSE for an anguilliform body than for a compact one, because a single frame very often contains only a mid-trunk segment with no head and no caudal — a region with almost no distinguishing GEOMETRY and strong translational ambiguity along the long axis, i.e. the matcher cannot tell which 30cm of a 2m animal it is looking at. DPFM's overlap predictor answers 'which region', but it answers it from geometry, and on a featureless cylindrical trunk there is little geometry to answer with. For a sevengill that ambiguity would have to be broken by the pigmentation pattern itself — which is the same conclusion reached under diffusionnet-2022: the geometric stage cannot carry identity alone, the speckle texture must be in the loop, and probably must be in the loop DURING correspondence rather than after it. Two further sevengill flags: the anchoring landmarks that would disambiguate along-axis position are exactly the ones the white-shark schema gets wrong (the single dorsal sits far posterior near the pelvics, there is no second dorsal, and the seven gill slits change the head signature), and the very long upper caudal lobe is a high-curvature non-isometric extremity. And GPL-3.0 is a live constraint on anything the lab redistributes.

The record is right that crease-awareness suits the trailing edges of the single posterior dorsal, the pectorals and the long upper caudal lobe. The stronger argument is the one it missed: an anguilliform lateral bend of a sevengill trunk is very nearly ISOMETRIC (shark skin is a near-inextensible helical-fibre corset; the body bends without stretching), so the genuine non-isometry in this problem is NOT the swimming pose — it is inter-individual variation (a 1.5 m juvenile vs a 3 m adult), jaw protrusion, and fin articulation. elongate_relevance: MEDIUM-HIGH. The input record's core argument is sound and I would keep it: a coarse-to-fine hierarchy that starts at only 6 eigenfunctions resolves gross anterior-posterior orientation BEFORE committing to fine correspondence, which is the precise failure mode on a near-cylindrical elongate body where every mid-trunk patch looks alike. The Sinkhorn/OT assignment adds a global bijectivity pressure that greedy nearest-neighbour lacks, again exactly what stops a template sliding along a shark's long axis. Two honest deductions from the record's optimism: (1) the smooth-shell embedding still leans near-isometric — acceptable for a bending sevengill trunk, which is close to isometric, but weaker for juvenile-vs-adult allometry; (2) at k_min=6 the low-order eigenfunctions of a high-aspect-ratio body are almost entirely long-axis modes, so the coarse level may carry very little circumferential (dorsal-vs-ventral, left-vs-right flank) information — and left/right flank disambiguation is essential for pigmentation-pattern re-ID, since a sevengill's spot pattern on the left flank is a different signature from the right. Untested on anything anguilliform. The included checkpoint is human-trained and would not transfer; the classical Smooth Shells variant in the same repo needs no training and is the more realistic first experiment on shark meshes.

citation: Thibault Groueix, Matthew Fisher, Vladimir G. Kim, Bryan C. Russell, Mathieu Aubry. "3D-CODED: 3D Correspondences by Deep Deformation". European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2018.

The template is the 6890-vertex SMPL human body mesh (SMPL is MPI-licensed, registration + EULA, non-commercial research only), and training uses SURREAL, which per its own repo requires accepting license terms with issued credentials before download (terms at di.ens.fr/willow/research/surreal/data/license.html). So: MIT code, EULA-gated non-commercial template and training data. Anyone reusing the released weights inherits those terms. Re-training on a lab-owned shark template would avoid the encumbrance — but see data_requirement for what that costs.
representation_3d: A single FIXED template mesh is deformed by a learned encoder-decoder (an AtlasNet-style point decoder conditioned on a global shape code) to fit each target point cloud or mesh. Dense correspondence is then read off for free through the template's fixed vertex indexing — every fitted shape inherits the template's vertex numbering, which is exactly the property a canonical-UV re-ID scheme needs. A test-time optimisation stage refines the regressed fit per instance.
supervision: Effectively unsupervised at the correspondence level: trained with a Chamfer reconstruction loss against target point clouds, with no correspondence annotations. NOTE the important asterisk the record glosses: the training corpus is SYNTHETIC (SURREAL, generated from SMPL with known parameters), so while no correspondence labels are consumed, the method depends on a large parametric-model-generated corpus — which is a data requirement, not a supervision-free lunch.
species_domain: Humans (SURREAL for training, FAUST for evaluation) and generic shape categories. No animals, no fish, nothing elongate.
data_requirement: THE MOST DECISION-RELEVANT NUMBERS IN THIS CHUNK, and I read them straight out of auxiliary/dataset.py rather than from prose: training set returns 230000 samples; test set returns 200; npoints defaults to 2500 points sampled per shape; the template is 6890 vertices (np.random.choice(6890, ...)). So the released recipe needs on the order of 230,000 training meshes generated from a parametric model of the target species. Contrast this with the other three entries in this chunk, which train on 50-80 meshes. Training wall-clock, GPU model and GPU-hours are NOT STATED in the README; test-time optimisation duration per shape is also NOT STATED there (both are in the ECCV paper, which the egress proxy blocked me from reading — I am not quoting numbers I did not see). SURREAL itself is 275GB across all modalities and is credential-gated. Images per individual / number of views / image resolution: N/A — this method consumes 3D point clouds and meshes, not images.
key_numbers: 230,000 SURREAL training shapes; 200 test shapes; 2500 points sampled per shape; 6890-vertex SMPL template. ECCV 2018. Reported FAUST correspondence errors NOT verified and not quoted.
elongate_relevance: HIGH on architecture fit, LOW on immediate feasibility — and the gap between those two is the honest finding. Architecture fit: this is by far the closest analogue to what shark-pose-3d already is. SharkSMPL is a fixed template plus LBS; 3D-CODED is a fixed template plus a learned free-form deformation, and it hands you dense correspondence for free from template indexing. Define UV once on the template and every fitted instance inherits it — no new surface-parameterization research needed. Template-based correspondence also makes NO isometry assumption, so large lateral bending is not intrinsically a problem. Feasibility blockers, stated plainly. (1) The 230,000-shape training requirement. The lab has ONE template mesh — a 3912-vertex DigitalLife3D GREAT WHITE — and generating 230k sevengill meshes requires first having a sevengill parametric model, which is the very thing being built. This is circular unless the corpus is bootstrapped from a hand-built rigged sevengill template with randomised shape/pose, which is achievable in Blender given the existing domain-randomisation pipeline but is a substantial asset-creation project, not a weekend. (2) SPECIES-TEMPLATE INVALIDITY, which the record does not flag hard enough: the white-shark template CANNOT be reused for Notorynchus cepedianus. A sevengill has seven gill slits not five, ONE dorsal fin set far posterior near the pelvics with NO second dorsal at all, a strongly heterocercal caudal with a very long upper lobe, and a broad blunt head on a far more anguilliform trunk. Retopologising the white-shark mesh will not produce a valid sevengill template; the second-dorsal region has no anatomical counterpart to map to. (3) The record correctly identifies the Chamfer-sliding failure — a Chamfer-only loss on a near-cylindrical body will happily slide the template along its own axis — and correctly proposes landmark anchors from the existing keypoint detector. But note the anchors available are FEWER than 16: first_dorsal_base and first_dorsal_tip must be re-defined as the single posterior dorsal, second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip are anatomically NULL for this species, and gill_slit is ambiguous across seven slits rather than five. Realistically ~13 usable anchors under a revised sevengill schema, and the existing YOLOv8n-pose weights (trained on white sharks, Pose mAP50 0.578) will not transfer without re-annotation.

CORRECTION TO INPUT RECORD'S FRAMING: the released pipeline is NOT a feed-forward UV predictor — it is a six-stage per-shape / per-pair optimisation: (1) SLIM parameterization as preprocessing, (2) oversampling via Meshlab midpoint subdivision, (3) surface overfitting, (4) neural parameterization, (5) two-surface map optimisation, (6) collection map optimisation. Verified from the official README.

Paper-level metrics unobtainable: arxiv.org, export.arxiv.org, openaccess.thecvf.com, semanticscholar, dblp, OpenAlex and Crossref are ALL egress-blocked in this session, so the PDF/abstract could not be read.

What it actually needs: (a) an input mesh — README says 'any mesh format' with no stated vertex budget; (b) a SLIM parameterization computed first, which requires the mesh to be CUT TO DISK TOPOLOGY (implied by the pipeline's dependence on SLIM, not stated verbatim in the README); (c) oversampling by Meshlab midpoint subdivision, ratio not specified; (d) a GPU (the environment requires a 'pytorch svd on gpu' package). elongate_relevance: MEDIUM-HIGH — cleanest formalism for stating the distortion objective explicitly, but it is a per-shape optimisation, not a per-frame pose-invariant mapper, so it solves the atlas problem and NOT the pose problem. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE INPUT RECORD. (1) The record's claim that 'an elongate shark trunk is close to a generalized cylinder, and a cylinder is developable, so the trunk admits a near-isometric flattening' is OVERSTATED and partly wrong as geometry: only a true (constant-radius) cylinder, cone, or tangent-developable has zero Gaussian curvature. A sevengill trunk TAPERS toward both the blunt head and the caudal peduncle, so Gaussian curvature is nonzero and the flattening is not near-isometric. The weaker true statement — an elongate tapering trunk flattens with far lower area/angle distortion than a compact or spherical body, and distortion concentrates at head, single posterior dorsal, pectorals and the long upper caudal lobe — is the one worth putting in the writeup. (2) The optional landmark constraints cannot be driven by the existing 16-keypoint white-shark Schema v2: second_dorsal_base and second_dorsal_tip DO NOT EXIST on Notorynchus cepedianus, first_dorsal_base/tip sit far posterior near the pelvics rather than mid-trunk, and 'gill_slit' is a single labelled point where there are seven slits. Any landmark set used here must be re-specified for the hexanchiform body plan before it constrains anything.

elongate_relevance: MEDIUM, and lower than the input record implies. The core technical argument survives and is correct: the Jacobian's singular values ARE exactly the local stretch factors, so predicting Jacobians is the right representation in which to write 'conformal on the trunk, area-distortion permitted at the fins' as an enforceable constraint — that matters because the sevengill identity signal (dark-on-light speckling on a grey-brown dorsum) lives on the trunk, and anisotropic shear there would smear the very pattern being matched. Two hard caveats the record missed. NJF is therefore a tool for a LATER stage, after a sevengill template and a deformation family exist.

code_url: none found — NO official implementation. The only code is an unofficial third-party reimplementation: https://github.com/ruiqixu37/Nuvo (self-described 'Personal Implementation of the paper', 46 stars, 2 forks, created 2024-06-03, last updated 2026-06-30). A GitHub repository search for 'Nuvo neural UV mapping unruly 3D representations' returned exactly ONE result — that reimplementation — which is strong evidence Google/DeepMind never released official code.

THIRD-PARTY REIMPLEMENTATION github.com/ruiqixu37/Nuvo: NONE FOUND — no LICENSE file (github.com/ruiqixu37/Nuvo/blob/main/LICENSE returns HTTP 404) and no license badge in the sidebar. Under default copyright that means ALL RIGHTS RESERVED: the lab has no grant to use, modify or redistribute it, for research OR commercially. Treat as legally unusable until the author adds a licence or is asked directly.
representation_3d: Neural UV mapping that jointly fits a chart decomposition plus a per-chart UV parameterization to geometry that is NOT a clean mesh (NeRF / volumetric / 'unruly' 3D representations), optimising for injectivity and low distortion. The third-party implementation additionally does vertex duplication by default to prevent texture interpolation artifacts across UV chart boundaries — which is itself an admission of how much the seams hurt.
supervision: Per-scene optimisation, self-supervised. No labels, no correspondence.
species_domain: Generic 3D scenes and objects. NOT animals. The third-party implementation's training data is 'Alec Jacobson's collection of 3D models' (the common-3d-test-models set), i.e. static geometry-processing benchmarks — no articulated subjects, no deforming subjects, no animals.
key_numbers: Paper's own numbers NOT OBTAINABLE — arxiv.org, export.arxiv.org, the project page pratulsrinivasan.github.io, huggingface.co, semanticscholar, dblp, OpenAlex and Crossref are ALL egress-blocked in this session. No distortion metrics, no chart counts, no optimisation times from the paper. From the third-party reimplementation's README only: Ubuntu 20.04, a single RTX 4090, Python 3.9, PyTorch 2.3.0 with CUDA 11.8. Training invoked as `python train.py --config configs/<config>.json`. No wall-clock time given.
data_requirement: No images per individual and no multi-view capture requirement in the usual sense — the input is a 3D representation (mesh or NeRF/volumetric field), and the output is a UV atlas for it. So the real requirement is UPSTREAM: you must already have a reconstructed sevengill 3D representation before Nuvo does anything, and producing that from 661GB of opportunistic dive video is the actual unsolved step. Hardware, from the reimplementation only: one RTX 4090, 24GB. GPU-hours: not stated anywhere I could read. Resolution, chart count, training-set size: not stated.
elongate_relevance: MEDIUM, with a specific and underappreciated failure mode for this species. Nuvo is the most recent statement of 'learn a UV atlas with explicit injectivity and distortion objectives on messy geometry', which is exactly the situation if sevengill geometry comes from a neural reconstruction rather than a clean artist template — that part of the input record's reasoning is sound. THE PROBLEM IS CHARTS. Nuvo decomposes the surface into MULTIPLE charts and then flattens each; on a long, laterally-bending, tapering trunk a chart decomposition will almost certainly cut ACROSS the trunk, placing seams straight through the dark-on-light speckle field that is the claimed identity signal. The reimplementation shipping vertex-duplication-by-default 'to prevent texture interpolation artifacts across UV chart boundaries' confirms seams are a live artifact, not a theoretical one. For re-ID you want ONE chart over the trunk with a stable, semantically-anchored (arc-length x circumference) frame so the same speckle lands at the same (u,v) across individuals and across dives — Nuvo optimises injectivity and distortion but has NO mechanism to make chart layout consistent across different reconstructions, so two dives of the same animal can get different atlases and the descriptors will not compare. SECOND LIMIT: Nuvo charts ONE STATIC geometry. It does nothing about pose. A sevengill's anguilliform lateral flexion is precisely the pose variation the whole research question is about, so Nuvo is at best the atlas stage downstream of a pose-canonicalising template — it is not itself an answer to pose-invariant re-ID. Combined with 'no official code' and 'reimplementation has no licence', I would rank this as reference-only for the lab, not adoptable.

Released car-category dataset is 33 GB. Pretrained models are provided via a `model_url` config option. Image resolution: NOT STATED in the README. GPU requirements and training duration: NOT STATED in the README. Paper-level metrics (SSIM/FID etc.) not obtainable — arxiv.org, export.arxiv.org, openaccess.thecvf.com and the aggregators are all egress-blocked in this session, so the PDF was never read.
data_requirement: HARD REQUIREMENTS, and this is the decisive point for the lab: per object you need 17 input views plus 10 further views WITH REGISTERED DEPTH MAPS AND KNOWN CAMERA POSES, plus the 3D geometry and a point cloud. That is a calibrated multi-view capture rig. Opportunistic single-camera dive footage of a free-swimming Notorynchus cepedianus supplies NONE of it — no depth, no calibrated extrinsics, no static subject to triangulate against, and the animal deforms between frames so multi-view stereo assumptions break outright. Dataset scale for reference: 33 GB for one ShapeNet category. GPU-hours not stated. Images per INDIVIDUAL for re-ID: not applicable — the method has no notion of individual identity.
elongate_relevance: LOW as a tool, MEDIUM as an argument — and I would keep it in the report for the second reason only, which is roughly what the input record already says, stated a bit more strongly. It is body-plan agnostic and was never aimed at animals, so it says nothing specific about a laterally-bending, seven-gill-slit, single-posterior-dorsal shark. Its value is as the explicit counter-proposal to UV atlasing: if you never flatten, you never pay a distortion or a seam cost, and for a long tapering trunk where a chart decomposition wants to cut across the speckle field (see the Nuvo entry), that is a real temptation. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS DECISIVE THOUGH, and it is the lab's own stack that decides it: comparing identity in a 3D texture field forfeits the entire 2D CNN/ViT toolchain. shark-scar-classifier is DINOv2 ViT-S/14, SharkScarAnnotator has a DINOv2-small 384-d extractor plumbed, and the lab's own prior pass recommended MiewID-msv3 / MegaDescriptor / WildFusion — every one of those consumes a 2D IMAGE. So the practical conclusion is: canonicalise pose on a template, then RASTERISE a UV image at the end and feed that to the existing descriptors. Texture Fields is the paper you cite to show you considered the no-flattening fork and rejected it for a stated reason. Its 17-view + depth + calibrated-camera data requirement independently rules it out for wild sevengill footage.

citation: Marie-Julie Rakotosaona, Paul Guerrero, Noam Aigerman, Niloy J. Mitra, Maks Ovsjanikov. "Learning Delaunay Surface Elements for Mesh Reconstruction." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), June 2021, pp. 22-31.
license: CC BY-NC 4.0 — 'Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License', stated verbatim in the fetched README. NON-COMMERCIAL: this bars any commercial deployment (paid consulting deliverable, commercial monitoring product, licensing the model to an operator) without separate permission from the authors. Also note CC licenses are written for creative works, not software, so patent and warranty terms are unclear for code — an additional reason to treat this as research-only. Fine for an academic sevengill study; a blocker for anything downstream that gets sold.
representation_3d: Three-stage pipeline on point clouds: (1) neural networks predict a local LOGARITHMIC MAP (logmap) at each point — a local 2D flattening of the surface neighbourhood; (2) logmaps from neighbouring points are aligned for consistency; (3) a triangle-selection step assembles a near-manifold mesh. The re-ID-relevant part is stage 1: a learned local canonical 2D frame at every surface point, with no global cut and no global distortion budget.
supervision: Supervised on synthetic ground-truth logmaps computed from meshes; at inference the reconstruction needs only a point cloud. Pretrained classifier and logmap checkpoints are released (trained on the 'famousthingi' dataset, download link in the README).
data_requirement: NOT STATED in the fetched README: number of training shapes, number of patches, epochs, GPU model, GPU-hours, or memory. Only qualitative guidance is given: 'For numerical precision reasons we suggest to use point clouds with a bounding box diagonal larger than 1'. The property that matters is real: local logmap frames are indifferent to global elongation and to lateral bending, which is exactly what an anguilliform, laterally-undulating sevengill trunk breaks in a global atlas. But three things cut against it. (1) The record's own stated cost is decisive for re-ID: purely local frames discard global layout, so you cannot tell an anterior flank spot cluster from an identical posterior one without a separate body-axis coordinate — and on a sevengill the natural anterior-posterior landmarks are precisely the ones your white-shark schema loses (no second dorsal, dorsal displaced far posterior, seven gill slits instead of five), so that extra mechanism is not free. (2) Using the logmap network as a general local-frame extractor for image-based pattern matching is a REPURPOSING the paper neither tests nor claims — it is trained and evaluated for meshing from clean point clouds, not for photographs of a swimming animal. citation: Xu Chen, Yufeng Zheng, Michael J. Black, Otmar Hilliges, Andreas Geiger. "SNARF: Differentiable Forward Skinning for Animating Non-rigid Neural Implicit Shapes." ICCV 2021. arXiv:2104.03953. Follow-up: Xu Chen, Tianjian Jiang, Jie Song, Max Rietmann, Andreas Geiger, Michael J. Black, Otmar Hilliges. "Fast-SNARF: A Fast Deformer for Articulated Neural Fields." IEEE TPAMI, 2023.

Black, Otmar Hilliges, Andreas Geiger; no non-commercial or research-only clause. fast-snarf README/repo: MIT. IMPORTANT CAVEAT, decision-relevant: the CODE is MIT but the pipeline is unusable without third-party assets that are NOT: SMPL body models (smpl.is.tue.mpg.de, academic registration + EULA, non-commercial), AMASS (DFaust-Synthetic and PosePrior subsets, SMPL-H format, registration), and CAPE (cape.is.tue.mpg.de, registration). representation_3d: Neural implicit occupancy field defined in a fixed CANONICAL pose space, plus differentiable FORWARD skinning with a learned continuous skinning-weight field. Deformation is canonical->posed; the correspondence for a posed query point is found by iterative root-finding, differentiated analytically via implicit differentiation. Because skinning is forward rather than backward, the canonical space does not absorb pose and the model generalises to unseen poses instead of memorising training poses.
supervision: Posed 3D scans / point clouds (or occupancy samples) with an accompanying skeleton / bone transforms. No canonical-space ground truth and no ground-truth skinning weights are required.
species_domain: Humans (minimally-clothed bodies from AMASS/DFaust; clothed bodies from CAPE). No animal experiments.
data_requirement: From the official repo README (verified): minimally-clothed human training ~12 hours on a single NVIDIA 2080Ti; clothed human (CAPE) training ~24 hours on a single 2080Ti. Fast-SNARF README (verified): ~25 minutes on a single 2080Ti for minimally clothed, ~1 hour for CAPE clothed - stated as 150x faster than SNARF. Training data = AMASS DFaust-Synthetic and PosePrior subsets and CAPE; the repos do not state a per-subject image count, number of views, or image resolution, because the input is 3D scans/point clouds, not images. Images per individual: not applicable / not stated. GPU-hours: 12-24 GPU-h (SNARF), ~0.4-1 GPU-h (Fast-SNARF), single consumer GPU.
elongate_relevance: high - forward skinning over an explicit kinematic tree is exactly what makes a canonical UV space pose-stable, and SharkSMPL is already a forward LBS model, so this is a drop-in stability argument rather than a new architecture. Two hard caveats for Notorynchus: (1) the white-shark 16-joint tree is the wrong skeleton - an anguilliform, laterally-undulating trunk needs several more fine axial joints between body_midpoint_dorsal and caudal_notch to represent high-curvature lateral bending without LBS candy-wrapper stretching, and stretching in the canonical map is precisely what destroys a pigmentation-pattern identity signature; (2) the second_dorsal_base / second_dorsal_tip joints and landmarks are anatomically meaningless on a sevengill (single dorsal, set far posterior near the pelvics) and the five-gill-slit landmark convention does not transfer to seven gill slits. SNARF itself is species-agnostic - it only needs a skeleton and posed geometry - but posed 3D shark scans/point clouds do not exist, so in practice this must be paired with a video-based method (lab4d/RAC) that discovers the geometry.
key_numbers: SNARF: 12h (minimal) / 24h (clothed) on one 2080Ti. Fast-SNARF: 25min / 1h on one 2080Ti, 150x speedup over SNARF (repo README). citation: Keunhong Park, Utkarsh Sinha, Jonathan T. Barron, Sofien Bouaziz, Dan B Goldman, Steven M. Seitz, Ricardo Martin-Brualla. "Nerfies: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields." ICCV 2021. Companion: Keunhong Park, Utkarsh Sinha, Peter Hedman, Jonathan T. Barron, Sofien Bouaziz, Dan B Goldman, Ricardo Martin-Brualla, Steven M. Seitz. "HyperNeRF: A Higher-Dimensional Representation for Topologically Varying Neural Radiance Fields." ACM Transactions on Graphics 40(6), December 2021.
license: Apache-2.0 for BOTH repos (confirmed on the GitHub repo pages). Both repositories were ARCHIVED and made read-only on 18 April 2026 - permissive license, but no upstream maintenance, and the codebase is JAX/Flax of that era, so expect dependency rot. No non-commercial clause on either.
representation_3d: A canonical template NeRF plus a per-observation continuous deformation field (SE(3) field) warping observed-space points back into the canonical frame, regularised by an elastic-energy prior, a background-rigidity loss, and coarse-to-fine positional-encoding annealing. HyperNeRF replaces the single canonical template with a template sliced from a higher-dimensional ambient space, so topological change is absorbed by movement along the ambient axis rather than by tearing the canonical template.
supervision: Self-supervised from casual monocular video (Nerfies: a handheld 'selfie' orbit) plus SfM camera poses; photometric reconstruction loss only. No masks, no keypoints, no template.
species_domain: Humans and everyday objects in casual monocular capture. No animals, no underwater.
data_requirement: From the official Nerfies repo README (verified): the paper's main configuration requires 8 GPUs; high-resolution training takes approximately 3 days on 8 GPUs (~576 GPU-hours); a lower-resolution variant takes approximately 14 hours on 8 GPUs (~112 GPU-hours). Capture: a single casual monocular video per scene (the paper's captures are handheld phone orbits); the repo does not state a minimum frame count, minimum number of distinct viewpoints, or an image resolution figure - 'not stated' in the README. HyperNeRF repo states only that the demo Colabs train on Cloud TPUs or Colab GPUs and are explicitly 'not the fully featured models'; full training compute is not stated in that README. Images per individual: not applicable (per-scene optimisation, one scene = one capture).
elongate_relevance: medium (as a cautionary reference, low as a method to adopt). This is the canonical-space-for-a-deforming-body reference AND the clearest warning against the free-deformation-field route for identity work. The Nerfies canonical space is fixed only up to the deformation field's gauge freedom - it is regularised (elastic/rigidity priors, coarse-to-fine annealing), not anchored to anatomy - so two independent optimisations of two separate sevengill sightings land in two different canonical spaces and their unwrapped pigmentation patterns are not directly comparable. That is fatal for a re-ID coordinate system, which must be the SAME coordinate system across encounters years apart. HyperNeRF is worse for this purpose, not better: the ambient dimension gives the model an explicit escape hatch to explain appearance change by ambient coordinate rather than by surface position, which is exactly the confound you do not want when the appearance IS the identity signal. For an anguilliform body the elastic regulariser is also weakest precisely where the displacements are largest (large-amplitude lateral undulation of the posterior trunk and the long upper caudal lobe). Practical conclusion for this lab: prefer a skeleton-anchored canonical space (SNARF / SharkSMPL / lab4d-RAC) over a free deformation field whenever the canonical coordinates must double as identity coordinates. Also both repos are now archived, so this is a reference to cite, not a dependency to take on.
key_numbers: 8 GPUs, ~3 days high-res / ~14 hours low-res (Nerfies repo README). Per-scene optimisation, monocular casual video input. Both repos archived read-only 2026-04-18.

AND Gengshan Yang, Chaoyang Wang, N. Dinesh Reddy, Deva Ramanan. "Reconstructing Animatable Categories from Videos." CVPR 2023. venue: CVPR 2022 (BANMo); CVPR 2023 (RAC); lab4d is a framework/codebase, not a venue
